movements.name: Victorian Print
movements.summary: Industrial print's first flood: wood type, chromolithography and ornament catalogues let every printer combine every style at once, loudly and cheaply.

principles.name: Every line a different face
principles.idea: Job printers set each line of a bill in a different display face and size, so the hierarchy came from variety and sheer scale rather than from a system.
principles.example: Darius Wells's wood type specimens, New York, from 1828, the toolkit behind the mid-century letterpress playbill

principles.name: Ornament as a grammar
principles.idea: Ornament was catalogued, compared and taught as a language with rules, rather than copied piecemeal from a single historical style.
principles.example: Owen Jones, The Grammar of Ornament, 1856

principles.name: Colour for the mass market
principles.idea: Chromolithography and colour wood-engraving put saturated colour into ordinary homes through cards, labels and children's books for the first time.
principles.example: Walter Crane and Edmund Evans, The Baby's Opera, 1877; Louis Prang's Christmas cards, from 1874

principles.name: Eclectic revivalism
principles.idea: Gothic, Egyptian, Moorish and Rococo motifs were mixed freely on one surface, with fidelity to the motif valued over unity of the whole.
principles.example: Owen Jones, Plans, Elevations, Sections and Details of the Alhambra, 1836-1845

movements.name: Arts and Crafts
movements.summary: A moral revolt against shoddy machine goods: unity of design and making, honest materials, and ornament drawn from nature and medieval craft.

principles.name: The designer makes
principles.idea: Design and production are one act; the designer should understand, and ideally practise, the craft that realises the drawing.
principles.example: Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co., founded 1861, where the partners designed and supervised their own glass, textiles and furniture

principles.name: Truth to materials
principles.idea: A pattern should reveal how it is made, whether block-printed, woven or hand-set, instead of imitating another medium.
principles.example: William Morris, Strawberry Thief, indigo-discharge block-printed textile, 1883

principles.name: Nature, stylised and repeated
principles.idea: Plants and birds are flattened into an interlocking repeat with strong structural rhythm, never naturalistic illusion.
principles.example: William Morris, Trellis wallpaper, designed 1862, issued 1864

principles.name: Useful and beautiful
principles.idea: Everyday objects deserve the same care as fine art; the decorative arts are not a lesser category.
principles.example: Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society, first exhibition, London, 1888

principles.name: The book as architecture
principles.idea: Title page, frame and text block are designed as one built structure.
principles.example: Arthur Heygate Mackmurdo, Wren's City Churches title page, 1883

movements.name: Japonisme
movements.summary: Western artists absorbed the Japanese woodblock print: flat colour, cropped asymmetric framing, the outline, and empty ground as an active element.

principles.name: Flat colour, bounded line
principles.idea: Areas of unmodelled colour are held by a confident contour, so the image reads as pattern and silhouette rather than modelled volume.

principles.name: The cropped frame
principles.idea: Figures are cut by the edge and viewed from high or oblique angles, so the frame feels like a glimpse rather than a stage.
principles.example: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Ambassadeurs: Aristide Bruant, 1892

principles.name: Empty ground
principles.idea: Large untouched areas of paper become part of the composition rather than leftover background.
principles.example: Aubrey Beardsley, The Peacock Skirt, from Salome, 1894

keyWorks.title: Le Japon artistique (journal, ed. Siegfried Bing)

movements.name: Art Nouveau
movements.summary: The first international style made for the street: the whiplash line, flat Japanese colour and the large-format lithographic poster as public art.

principles.name: The whiplash line
principles.idea: A single sinuous, accelerating contour organises the whole sheet: hair, smoke, stems and lettering all follow the same curve.
principles.example: Alphonse Mucha, Job cigarette papers poster, 1896

principles.name: The poster as street art
principles.idea: Large colour lithographs treat the wall as a gallery and the figure as a seductive brand ambassador.
principles.example: Jules Chéret, Bal au Moulin Rouge, 1889

principles.name: Silhouette over shading
principles.idea: Flat areas of colour and a few contours carry the image, so it reads from across a boulevard.
principles.example: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Moulin Rouge: La Goulue, 1891

principles.name: Lettering as ornament
principles.idea: Hand-drawn letters are shaped to fit the composition and share its line, not typeset in a separate band.
principles.example: Will Bradley, The Chap-Book: The Twins, 1894

principles.name: The halo and the frame
principles.idea: A circular nimbus or arched mosaic frame isolates the figure like an icon and makes a repeatable format.

movements.name: Glasgow Style
movements.summary: Glasgow's austere strand of Art Nouveau: elongated figures, the rose motif and rectilinear grids that pointed Vienna toward geometry.

principles.name: Verticality
principles.idea: Figures and forms are stretched into tall, column-like shapes that turn the poster into a narrow architectural elevation.
principles.example: Charles Rennie Mackintosh, The Scottish Musical Review, 1896

principles.name: Curve held by the grid
principles.idea: Organic motifs are boxed by straight lines and squares, so the curve is ornament and the rectangle is structure.
principles.example: Mackintosh, Glasgow School of Art, north facade and library, 1897-1909

principles.name: The stylised rose
principles.idea: One reduced, repeatable motif, the cabbage rose, travels across posters, stencils, gesso and furniture as a house mark.
principles.example: Margaret Macdonald, The May Queen gesso panel, 1900

principles.name: The room as one work
principles.idea: Lettering, stencils, furniture and cutlery are designed as one environment, keyed to a restricted palette of white, mauve and silver.
principles.example: Mackintosh and Macdonald, Willow Tea Rooms, Room de Luxe, 1903

movements.name: Private Press Movement
movements.summary: Small presses rebuilt the book from the type up, reviving incunabula-era type, handmade paper and the double-page spread as the unit of design.

principles.name: The spread is the unit
principles.idea: Design the two facing pages together, with margins graduated inner, top, outer and bottom so the two text blocks read as one composition.
principles.example: Kelmscott Press, The Works of Geoffrey Chaucer, 1896

principles.name: Type from the source
principles.idea: Redraw a typeface from the strongest historical model, here Jenson's 1470s roman, rather than from the weakened commercial faces of the day.

principles.name: Dense, even colour
principles.idea: Tight word spacing and heavy type make the page an even dark texture, a counter to thin, grey Victorian book pages.
principles.example: Kelmscott Press, The Story of the Glittering Plain, 1891

principles.name: Austerity as luxury
principles.idea: The second wave stripped ornament out entirely and let a fine roman, generous margins and perfect presswork carry the book.

movements.name: Jugendstil
movements.summary: Germany's Art Nouveau, named after the magazine Jugend, moved from floral line toward abstraction, new typefaces and industrial design.

principles.name: The magazine as laboratory
principles.idea: Weekly and quarterly art magazines changed their cover art every issue, making the periodical a running test bed for the style.
principles.example: Jugend, Munich, founded by Georg Hirth, 1896

principles.name: Typefaces drawn with a brush
principles.idea: Letterforms adopt the swelling, plant-like stroke of the ornament so that type and image belong to one hand.

principles.name: From curve to abstraction
principles.idea: Natural forms are pushed toward pure abstract line and later toward geometric rigour.
principles.example: Peter Behrens, Der Kuss, colour woodcut for Pan, 1898

principles.name: The artists' colony
principles.idea: A designed community where architecture, furniture, books and exhibition were one demonstration of a new way of living.
principles.example: Darmstadt Artists' Colony exhibition, Ein Dokument deutscher Kunst, 1901

images.title: Jugend, no. 14
images.credit: Otto Eckmann (1865-1902) (signature E O (monogram) at bottom left)

movements.name: Vienna Secession
movements.summary: Vienna's break from the academy turned Art Nouveau's curve into the square: modular grids, block lettering and the total work of art.

principles.name: The square module
principles.idea: The square and the grid replace the whiplash as the organising unit, from page layouts to perforated metal to whole buildings.
principles.example: Josef Hoffmann, Gitterwerk perforated metal objects, Wiener Werkstätte, c. 1904

principles.name: Lettering as architecture
principles.idea: Letters are drawn as blocky, condensed shapes fitted into rectangles, so the type itself becomes a structural field.
principles.example: Koloman Moser, poster for the 13th Secession exhibition, 1902

principles.name: Flat field, precise figure
principles.idea: Large areas of flat colour or empty paper are punctuated by a small, exactly placed figurative or ornamental element.
principles.example: Gustav Klimt, poster for the 1st Secession exhibition, 1898

principles.name: Gesamtkunstwerk
principles.idea: Exhibition, building, magazine, furniture and cutlery are designed as one coherent work.
principles.example: 14th Secession exhibition (Beethoven), installed by Josef Hoffmann with Klimt's Beethoven Frieze, 1902

principles.name: The maker's mark as identity
principles.idea: Monograms and marks for the designer, the craftsman and the workshop are stamped on every object, an early system of brand marks.
principles.example: Wiener Werkstätte rose mark and monograms, 1903

movements.name: Plakatstil
movements.summary: Berlin's object poster reduced advertising to one product, one or two words and a few flat colours, the first modern brand language.

principles.name: The object is the message
principles.idea: Show the product itself, alone and large, with no scene, no figure and no slogan.

principles.name: One word
principles.idea: The brand name, set in heavy hand-drawn capitals, is the entire text.

principles.name: Flat colour, few colours
principles.idea: Two to four flat lithographic colours against a strong ground give a sheet that reads in a second from a moving tram.

principles.name: Pattern and light as texture
principles.idea: In the Munich variant, the figure dissolves into flat interlocking patches of light and shadow that read as tone without modelling.

movements.name: Expressionism
movements.summary: German artists revived the raw woodcut and distorted colour to carry emotion; the early Bauhaus began inside it.

principles.name: The cut shows
principles.idea: The gouge mark of the woodblock is the expression; nothing is smoothed away.
principles.example: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Brücke programme and membership woodcuts, 1905–1906

principles.name: Emotion over description
principles.idea: Colour and distortion carry feeling rather than likeness.
principles.example: Kandinsky & Marc, Der Blaue Reiter almanac, 1912

principles.name: Image and lettering as one block
principles.idea: Letters are carved with the picture, so type inherits the image's roughness.
principles.example: Lyonel Feininger, Cathedral woodcut, Bauhaus manifesto cover, 1919

movements.name: Futurism
movements.summary: Marinetti's cult of speed and the machine exploded the printed page into words-in-freedom, typography performed as sound.

principles.name: Typography as sound
principles.idea: Size, weight and face render loudness, onomatopoeia and rhythm, so the page is performed rather than read.

principles.name: Destroy the horizontal line
principles.idea: Words run diagonally, curve and radiate; the reading path is the composition.
principles.example: F.T. Marinetti, Les mots en liberté futuristes, 1919

principles.name: Many typefaces on one page
principles.idea: Mixing faces and ink colours is the point, against classical typographic harmony.

principles.name: The book as object
principles.idea: Binding, material and format are part of the message.
principles.example: Fortunato Depero, Depero futurista (the bolted book), 1927

principles.name: Advertising is art
principles.idea: Commerce is treated as modern life's real theatre.

images.title: Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash
Unique Forms of Continuity in Space

movements.name: Vorticism
movements.summary: London's hard-edged riposte to Futurism, best remembered for BLAST's magenta cover and shouting slabs of black grotesque type.

principles.name: Bless and blast
principles.idea: Lists of heroes and enemies used as layout; the magazine page as polemic.

principles.name: Typographic shouting
principles.idea: Huge black condensed grotesque caps set in dense stacked blocks.
principles.example: BLAST no. 1 cover and manifesto pages, 1914

principles.name: The vortex
principles.idea: Hard-edged angular abstraction around a still centre rather than Futurist blur.

movements.name: Suprematism
movements.summary: Malevich reduced painting to floating geometric planes on white, a grammar of pure form that Constructivism turned to use.

principles.name: The zero of form
principles.idea: Strip painting to elementary shapes on white; pure feeling, no object.

principles.name: Floating planes in infinite space
principles.idea: No horizon or gravity; forms drift at angles in an open white field.
principles.example: Kazimir Malevich, Suprematist Composition: Airplane Flying, 1915

principles.name: A grammar of elements
principles.idea: Square, circle, cross and bar as a teachable vocabulary.
principles.example: Kazimir Malevich, The Non-Objective World, Bauhaus Book 11, 1927

principles.name: Abstract forms can narrate
principles.idea: Geometric shapes act as characters in a story.

keyWorks.title: From Cubism and Futurism to Suprematism

movements.name: Constructivism
movements.summary: Soviet artists recast themselves as constructors of the new society, inventing the photomontage poster and the engineered page.

principles.name: Art into production
principles.idea: The designer is an engineer making useful things for mass life: posters, books, textiles, kiosks.

principles.name: Photomontage and factography
principles.idea: Photography replaces drawing because it is documentary and mass-reproducible.

principles.name: The diagonal as revolutionary energy
principles.idea: Compositions on tilted axes in stark red and black.
principles.example: El Lissitzky, Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge, 1919

principles.name: The page as built space
principles.idea: Bars, rules and blocks of type act as structural members.
principles.example: El Lissitzky, Dlia golosa (For the Voice), 1923

keyWorks.title: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge
Let Us Fulfill the Plan of Great Works

movements.name: Dada
movements.summary: An anti-art revolt against the First World War that gave design photomontage, found-print collage and typographic anarchy.

principles.name: Found material over drawn image
principles.idea: Cut up the mass media and reassemble it to say what it hides.
principles.example: Hannah Höch, Cut with the Kitchen Knife, 1919–1920

principles.name: Photomontage as weapon
principles.idea: Recombined photographs make political lies visible with documentary authority.
principles.example: John Heartfield, Adolf, the Superman: Swallows Gold and Spouts Junk, AIZ, 1932

principles.name: Typography without hierarchy
principles.idea: Mixed faces, sizes and directions ambush the reader.
principles.example: Hugo Ball, Karawane, printed in the Dada Almanach, 1920

principles.name: Everything is material
principles.idea: Tickets, adverts and bank letterheads are as valid as paint.

keyWorks.title: Cut with the Kitchen Knife Dada Through the Last Weimar Beer-Belly Cultural Epoch of Germany

movements.name: De Stijl
movements.summary: Dutch artists sought universal harmony in orthogonal lines and primary colours, building letters, chairs and pages from rectangles.

principles.name: Only orthogonals and primaries
principles.idea: Red, yellow and blue plus black, white and grey, in rectangles bounded by straight lines.
principles.example: Piet Mondrian, Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow, 1930

principles.name: Letters built from the grid
principles.idea: The alphabet is constructed from rectangles, so type shares the composition's structure.

principles.name: Asymmetric equilibrium
principles.idea: Unequal parts held in balance, never centred.
principles.example: Gerrit Rietveld, Red Blue Chair, c. 1918–1923

principles.name: The diagonal as dynamism
principles.idea: Elementarism tilts the grid 45 degrees to add energy, splitting the group.

keyWorks.title: Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow

movements.name: Bauhaus
movements.summary: The German school that fused art, craft and industry and taught sans serif, photography and the foundation course to the world.

principles.name: Unity of the arts
principles.idea: Every discipline serves a shared built whole, under architecture.

principles.name: Learn from materials first
principles.idea: A preliminary course in form, colour and material comes before any specialism.

principles.name: Design for industry
principles.idea: Make prototypes for mass production, not crafts for the few.

principles.name: Elementary type
principles.idea: Sans serif, lowercase, rules and photographs as the modern print vocabulary.

principles.name: Typophoto
principles.idea: Text and image composed as a single visual statement.

movements.name: Art Deco
movements.summary: Commercial, glamorous modernism: Cubist and Futurist geometry turned into airbrushed posters for trains, liners and aperitifs.

principles.name: Geometric stylisation for speed
principles.idea: Subjects reduced to a few planes and a single vanishing point, read in an instant.

principles.name: Lettering from the image's geometry
principles.idea: Custom display type is built from the same forms as the picture.

principles.name: Monumentality through scale
principles.idea: Low viewpoint, huge object, tiny human.

principles.name: Serial storytelling
principles.idea: Images in sequence for viewers in motion.

principles.name: Avant-garde forms for mass commerce
principles.idea: Abstraction made desirable and used to sell.
principles.example: E. McKnight Kauffer, Soaring to Success! Daily Herald – the Early Bird, 1918–1919

keyWorks.title: Exposition internationale des arts décoratifs et industriels modernes
Power, the Nerve Centre of London's Underground

images.title: Brightest London is Best Reached by Underground

movements.name: Czech Avant-garde
movements.summary: Devětsil's Poetism turned Constructivist type, photomontage and the picture poem into a playful, lyrical modernism; Teige and Sutnar made it typography.

principles.name: The picture poem
principles.idea: Image and verse share one surface; the page is a canvas, not a column of text.
principles.example: Karel Teige, typography for Jaroslav Seifert's Na vlnách TSF, 1925

principles.name: Letters as bodies
principles.idea: The alphabet is performed: each letter staged as a pose and a photomontage.

principles.name: Constructivist economy for a lyrical end
principles.idea: Sans-serifs, bars and photographs used for joy and everyday modern life rather than agitation.
principles.example: Karel Teige, covers for ReD (Revue Devětsilu), 1927–1931

principles.name: Type alone holds attention
principles.idea: A strict hierarchy of type sizes replaces the picture.
principles.example: Ladislav Sutnar, Visit the Modern Textile Exhibition poster, 1930

images.title: Pozdrav z cesty (Greetings from the Journey)

movements.name: Chinese Modern Design
movements.summary: From Shanghai calendar posters and New Culture covers through the PRC propaganda poster to Hong Kong's cross-cultural identity and contemporary Chinese book design.

principles.name: Commerce as modernity's first language
principles.idea: In China modern visual culture arrived through advertising before it arrived through art schools.
principles.example: Shanghai yuefenpai calendar posters for British American Tobacco and Nanyang Brothers, 1920s-1930s

principles.name: The cover as manifesto
principles.idea: The book jacket was where the New Culture movement looked modern, with abstract motifs and hand-drawn characters.
principles.example: Tao Yuanqing, cover for Lu Xun's Panghuang (Wandering), 1926

principles.name: Satire through the graphic line
principles.idea: Caricature, Deco geometry and photomontage as political commentary under censorship.
principles.example: Zhang Guangyu, Journey to the West caricature cycle, 1945

principles.name: Image as mass mobilisation
principles.idea: One authorised image reproduced without limit, in saturated red with heroic faces and radiant light.
principles.example: Liu Chunhua, Chairman Mao Goes to Anyuan, 1967, reproduced some 900 million times

principles.name: Cross-cultural synthesis
principles.idea: Translate one specific Chinese form into modernist geometry for an international audience, rather than blending cultures into pastiche.
principles.example: Kan Tai-keung, Bank of China symbol, 1980

movements.name: New Typography
movements.summary: Tschichold codified the avant-garde for the printing trade: asymmetry, sans serif, photography and standard formats in the service of clarity.

principles.name: Clarity as purpose
principles.idea: Form is derived from the function of the message, not from tradition.

principles.name: Asymmetry over the central axis
principles.idea: Arrange by reading order and importance instead of the symmetrical title page.

principles.name: Sans serif as the face of the age
principles.idea: Geometric and grotesque sans faces replace blackletter and historic romans.

principles.name: Standardisation
principles.idea: DIN paper sizes and standard letterheads, envelopes and forms.
principles.example: Jan Tschichold, DIN letterhead schemes in Die neue Typographie, 1928

principles.name: Photography and white space as structure
principles.idea: Photographs replace illustration; rules and empty space organise the page.

movements.name: Isotype
aka: International System of Typographic Picture Education
movements.summary: A team method for turning social statistics into rows of standard pictograms anyone could read, the root of modern information design.

principles.name: Repetition, not scale
principles.idea: A greater quantity is shown by more symbols, never by a bigger symbol.

principles.name: Transformation
principles.idea: Analyse the data and decide what it should say before anything is drawn.
principles.example: Marie Neurath (Reidemeister), charts for the Vienna museum, from 1925

principles.name: Standardised pictograms
principles.idea: One reduced, consistent symbol per concept, combinable with others.
principles.example: Gerd Arntz, Isotype pictogram library, about 4,000 signs, from 1928

principles.name: A picture language for everyone
principles.idea: Charts that cross language and literacy barriers.

movements.name: American Modernism
movements.summary: European avant-garde form, carried by émigrés and adopted by American business, stripped of ideology and turned into a tool for clarity and impact.

principles.name: Form without the manifesto
principles.idea: The avant-garde toolkit of asymmetry, sans-serif, photomontage and primary colour is adopted for clarity and impact, not as a social programme.
principles.example: Lester Beall, Rural Electrification Administration posters, 1937

principles.name: The photograph as raw material
principles.idea: Photographs are cropped hard, bled, scaled against each other and made to converse with type rather than framed as pictures.
principles.example: Alexey Brodovitch, Harper's Bazaar spreads, from 1934

principles.name: White space is active
principles.idea: Emptiness is the frame that makes the one element on the page loud.

principles.name: Information as architecture
principles.idea: Large bodies of facts are organised by signs, tabs, grids and colour so a reader can navigate rather than merely read.
principles.example: Ladislav Sutnar and Knud Lönberg-Holm, Catalog Design, 1944

principles.name: Enlightened patronage
principles.idea: A company commissions art rather than advertising and lets the artist sign it, buying an image of intelligence.
principles.example: Container Corporation of America, Great Ideas of Western Man campaign, from 1950

images.title: America Calling
images.credit: Artist: Herbert Matter. Photographer: Arthur H. Fisher.

movements.name: Italian Modernism
movements.summary: Corporate modernism around Olivetti, Pirelli and La Rinascente: Swiss tools with Italian colour, wit and sculptural products.

principles.name: Culture as identity
principles.idea: A company's identity is everything it makes and commissions: products, buildings, ads, art.
principles.example: MoMA, Olivetti: Design in Industry exhibition, 1952

principles.name: Abstraction that seduces
principles.idea: Abstract shapes, numerals and colour express what a product does instead of depicting it.

principles.name: Sculptural products
principles.idea: The industrial object as one soft, unified sculpture around its mechanism.

principles.name: Kinetic, layered typography
principles.idea: Type and colour overprinted as transparent planes to suggest speed and depth.
principles.example: Max Huber, Gran Premio dell'Autodromo di Monza poster, 1948

movements.name: Taller de Gráfica Popular
movements.summary: A Mexico City print collective that made the linocut and woodcut a cheap, fast, collective broadside medium for labour, anti-fascist and revolutionary causes.

principles.name: The cheapest block wins
principles.idea: Linoleum and wood blocks cut fast and print on any paper, so a message could go from meeting to wall in days without a commercial printer.
principles.example: TGP broadsides and handbills of the Cárdenas years, from 1937

principles.name: Collective authorship
principles.idea: Work was often made collaboratively and editions were deliberately left unnumbered, refusing the collectible-print economy.
principles.example: TGP portfolios sold under the La Estampa Mexicana imprint

principles.name: The vernacular as the source
principles.idea: The popular broadside and the calavera of José Guadalupe Posada and Manuel Manilla, not academic art, set the visual language.
principles.example: TGP's revival of the satirical calavera, 1940s

principles.name: Narrative in black and white
principles.idea: Dense gouged blacks, figures massed in crowds and a single strong diagonal tell a political story in one image without colour.
principles.example: Leopoldo Méndez, En el nombre de Cristo, lithographs, 1942

keyWorks.title: En el nombre de Cristo (series of seven lithographs)

movements.name: Midcentury Modern
movements.summary: Postwar American design where new materials, furniture makers' patronage and a playful West Coast spirit joined furniture, film, exhibition and graphics.

principles.name: The material leads the form
principles.idea: New processes produce new shapes, and the object shows how it was made.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, LCW moulded-plywood chair, 1946

principles.name: Design within constraints
principles.idea: The designer's skill is recognising every constraint and working within it with enthusiasm.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, Eames House from off-the-shelf industrial parts, 1949

principles.name: One discipline across media
principles.idea: The same office makes chairs, toys, films, exhibitions and graphics with one sensibility.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, Mathematica exhibition, 1961

principles.name: Play as method
principles.idea: Toys, games and collections are treated as serious design research.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, House of Cards, 1952

principles.name: Explain with film and exhibition
principles.idea: Complex ideas are taught through multi-screen film and walk-through shows.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, Glimpses of the USA, Moscow, 1959

movements.name: New York School
aka: New York School of graphic design
movements.summary: American-born designers made the émigré toolkit witty and argumentative: one visual idea, often a pun, carrying the whole message.

principles.name: The idea is the design
principles.idea: A single compressible concept, visual or verbal, carries the communication; style only serves it.
principles.example: Paul Rand, Eye-Bee-M poster for IBM, 1981

principles.name: Wit and the visual pun
principles.idea: Juxtaposition and double meaning make the viewer complete the message and remember it.
principles.example: Doyle Dane Bernbach (art director Helmut Krone), Think Small Volkswagen ad, 1959

principles.name: Word and image as one
principles.idea: Copy and picture are conceived together, often by art director and copywriter in the same room.
principles.example: George Lois, Muhammad Ali as Saint Sebastian, Esquire cover, 1968

principles.name: The handmade inside the modern
principles.idea: Collage, torn paper, brush lettering and childlike drawing loosen an otherwise spare modern page.
principles.example: Saul Bass, The Man with the Golden Arm poster, 1955

principles.name: Simplify to the symbol

movements.name: Argentine Modernism
movements.summary: From the 1945 Arte Concreto-Invención group to the Di Tella design department and the 1971-72 Buenos Aires signage plan: invention, then system.

principles.name: Invent, don't represent
principles.idea: The invencionistas rejected illusion and symbolism: a work is a concrete object of colour, plane and line, not a picture of something else.

principles.name: Theory travels in print
principles.idea: A small magazine can carry a whole design culture across a continent by publishing art, architecture, industrial design and typography side by side.
principles.example: Nueva Visión, edited by Tomás Maldonado and Alfredo Hlito, 1951-1957

principles.name: One house, one voice
principles.idea: An institution's posters, catalogues and programmes share a single visual identity produced by an in-house department, mixing Swiss order with New York wit.
principles.example: Departamento de Diseño Gráfico, Instituto Di Tella, formalised 1963 under Juan Carlos Distéfano

principles.name: Design the street
principles.idea: A city's signs, street names and public information are one coherent system, designed as public infrastructure rather than as individual objects.
principles.example: González Ruiz and Shakespear, Plan Visual de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, 1971-1972

movements.name: Polish Poster School
movements.summary: State-commissioned film, theatre and circus posters where one authored, painterly metaphor and hand-drawn lettering replaced the star portrait and the grid.

principles.name: The poster as authored picture
principles.idea: The designer is also the image-maker; the personal hand is the point, not a house style.
principles.example: Henryk Tomaszewski, Obywatel Kane (Citizen Kane) poster, 1948

principles.name: Metaphor over depiction
principles.idea: One shortcut image stands for the whole film or play; indirection also passed the censor.

principles.name: Hand-lettering as image
principles.idea: Type is drawn, not set, and often carries the whole composition.

principles.name: Painterly gesture in print
principles.idea: Gouache, crayon, collage and photomontage go straight into offset lithography.
principles.example: Waldemar Świerzy, Czerwona Oberża (The Red Inn) poster, 1955

principles.name: Style follows the subject
principles.idea: No enforced style: baroque, art-nouveau line and halftone montage all belong.

movements.name: Arabic Modernism
movements.summary: Making Arabic script work with modern machines and media: type reform, Cairo and Beirut book and children's design, bilingual type and research.

principles.name: Simplify for the machine, keep the identity
principles.idea: Reduce contextual forms for print while keeping letters recognisable.
principles.example: Nasri Khattar, Unified Arabic, patented 1947, launched 1957

principles.name: The book cover as public art
principles.idea: A single illustrator's hand across thousands of covers becomes a shared visual language.
principles.example: Helmi El Touni, more than 3,000 book covers for Cairo and Beirut publishers

principles.name: Children's design as cultural sovereignty
principles.idea: Arab children's books written and drawn in the region, not translated.
principles.example: Mohieddine Ellabbad, Dar al-Fata al-Arabi, founded 1974

principles.name: Bilingual parity
principles.idea: Arabic and Latin designed together as equals, not Arabic retrofitted.

principles.name: Research as design
principles.idea: Writing the script's design history is part of the practice.
principles.example: Huda Smitshuijzen AbiFarès, Arabic Typography: A Comprehensive Sourcebook, 2001

movements.name: Hurufiyya
movements.summary: Pan-Arab and Islamic-world movement freeing Arabic calligraphy from classical rules and using letters as abstract signs of post-colonial identity.

principles.name: Free the letter from the rules
principles.idea: Classical proportion and devotional use are broken; the letter is distorted and abstracted.
principles.example: Madiha Omar, 22 calligraphy-based paintings, Georgetown Public Library, Washington, 1949

principles.name: The letter as sign, emptied and refilled
principles.idea: A character keeps its cultural link while losing its linguistic function.
principles.example: Shakir Hassan Al Said, One Dimension Group manifesto, Baghdad, 1971

principles.name: Geometry as a bridge
principles.idea: Kufic and the square link Islamic pattern, icon and architecture.

principles.name: Generations
principles.idea: Nationalist pioneers, then exiles, then a third generation using script purely abstractly.

movements.name: Swiss Style
movements.summary: Grid-built, objective typography from Zürich and Basel: one sans-serif, asymmetric layouts and documentary photography, presented as neutral public communication.

principles.name: The grid as constitution
principles.idea: A modular grid fixed before content arrives governs the size and position of every element.

principles.name: Objectivity over persuasion
principles.idea: Present information, don't cajole: neutral type, documentary photography, no illustration.
principles.example: Josef Müller-Brockmann, schützt das Kind! poster, 1953

principles.name: Asymmetry and active white space
principles.idea: Dynamic asymmetric composition in which empty space is structural, not leftover.

principles.name: One sans-serif, flush left
principles.idea: A single grotesque family in few weights and sizes, set ragged-right so spacing stays even.

principles.name: Elementary means
principles.idea: Build the poster from the simplest elements and a single strong contrast.

movements.name: Brazilian Concretism
movements.summary: Concrete painting, the Noigandres poets and Ulm-trained designers turned Brazil's industrial boom into a geometric, word-as-object visual culture and a national identity practice.

principles.name: The word is a thing
principles.idea: A poem is a visual-verbal object built from the space of the page; syntax is replaced by spatial arrangement, so typography carries the meaning.

principles.name: The sign without the name

principles.name: Teach it as a discipline

principles.name: The nation as client

movements.name: Japanese Modernism
movements.summary: Postwar Japan's corporate and national modernism: one bold geometric mark, objective photography, and design built as public infrastructure, crowned by Tokyo 1964.

principles.name: One mark carries the idea
principles.idea: Reduce a nation, event or company to a single geometric statement large enough to fill a poster.

principles.name: Photography as proof of modernity
principles.idea: Use the camera's objectivity and technical difficulty as the message itself.
principles.example: Kamekura and Osamu Hayasaki, Tokyo 1964 sprinter poster, 1962

principles.name: Tradition as geometry
principles.idea: Abstract historical Japanese forms such as Rinpa colour fields, crests and Noh masks into flat geometric elements on a modernist grid.

principles.name: Design as infrastructure
principles.idea: Design is a public system for everyone, including people who cannot read the language.
principles.example: Tokyo 1964 sport pictograms, Yoshiro Yamashita under Masaru Katsumi, 1963

principles.name: The designer as institution-builder

movements.summary: National and multinational companies adopted a simple symbol plus a written standards manual, so one visual system could run across everything they touched.

principles.name: The mark as irreducible symbol
principles.idea: A simple, often abstract mark can stand for a vast and complex company.

principles.name: The standards manual
principles.idea: Rules for colour, type, spacing and applications are written down so thousands of people apply the identity consistently.

principles.name: Total design
principles.idea: Graphics, products, architecture and environments speak one language under one design director.
principles.example: IBM design programme under Eliot Noyes with Paul Rand, from 1956

principles.name: Longevity over fashion

movements.name: Venezuelan Modernism
movements.summary: Oil-funded Caracas, where émigré designers and kinetic artists made corporate magazines, museum catalogues and alphabets into experiments in perception and print.

principles.name: The magazine as laboratory
principles.idea: A corporate house magazine, freed from selling, becomes a place to test paper, folds, screens and typographic structure issue by issue.
principles.example: El Farol (Creole Petroleum), art-directed by Gerd Leufert 1957-1959 and Nedo 1959-1972

principles.name: Exhibit the discipline
principles.idea: Showing design in a museum establishes it as a culture in its own right, not a by-product of advertising.
principles.example: Gráfica 1, Museo de Bellas Artes, Caracas, 1961, the country's first graphic design exhibition

principles.name: Perception as material
principles.idea: Colour and line are treated as events that change with the viewer's movement, not as fixed fills.

principles.name: Letters as impossible objects
principles.idea: An alphabet can be a geometric puzzle: reversible, impossible or computable forms that still read.

movements.name: Ulm School
movements.summary: Post-war German design college that replaced Bauhaus artistry with science, semiotics and systems, producing Braun's product language and Lufthansa's identity.

principles.name: Design as science
principles.idea: Decisions are justified by analysis of use, production, perception and sign, not by taste.
principles.example: Otl Aicher and development group E5, Lufthansa identity, 1962

principles.name: The system over the object
principles.idea: Design modular families and systems rather than single pieces.
principles.example: Hans Gugelot, M125 storage system for Bofinger, developed from 1950

principles.name: Semiotics in practice
principles.idea: Every graphic and product element is a sign with syntactic, semantic and pragmatic dimensions.
principles.example: Tomás Maldonado and Gui Bonsiepe, Olivetti/Rinascente coding system, 1964-67

principles.name: Social responsibility
principles.idea: Design is a political act with consequences, not commercial styling.
principles.example: HfG Ulm founded by the Scholl Foundation as a democratic institution, 1953

movements.name: Push Pin Style
movements.summary: Illustrator-designers who answered modernist correctness by raiding Victoriana, Art Nouveau, Deco and comics, with wit, bulbous line and flat colour.

principles.name: History as a toolbox
principles.idea: Any past style can be revived, reinterpreted and combined to serve a new idea.

principles.name: Illustration is design
principles.idea: Drawing, type and concept are made by one hand as one object.
principles.example: Seymour Chwast, End Bad Breath poster, 1967

principles.name: Wit over neutrality
principles.idea: Humour and irony replace modernist objectivity.
principles.example: Push Pin Studios, The Push Pin Graphic, from 1957

principles.name: Display type as personality
principles.idea: Custom phototype display faces give every job its own voice.

movements.name: Dutch Modernism
movements.summary: Amsterdam's grid-led, technology-minded modernism: visible grids, machine-drawn lettering and total identity programmes for museums, airports and the state.

principles.name: The grid made visible
principles.idea: The grid is printed as part of the image rather than hidden beneath it.
principles.example: Wim Crouwel, Vormgevers poster, Stedelijk Museum, 1968

principles.name: Type for the machine
principles.idea: Letterforms drawn to the limits of a new display technology, not against them.

principles.name: Total identity
principles.idea: One studio shapes graphics, interiors, signage and products so the environment speaks with one voice.
principles.example: Benno Wissing / Total Design, Schiphol Airport signage, 1967

principles.name: Playful rigour
principles.idea: Systematic work can be bright, witty and experimental.

movements.name: Functionalist Product Design
movements.summary: Braun's restrained, systematic appliances and Vitsœ's furniture systems: neutral bodies, colour only as signal, products as quiet tools.

principles.name: Form follows use
principles.idea: An appliance is a tool; its form comes from what the user does with it.
principles.example: Dieter Rams, Braun T3 pocket radio, 1958

principles.name: Colour as signal
principles.idea: Neutral bodies; colour reserved for the one control that matters.

principles.name: Systems, not products
principles.idea: Components that add up, last for decades and can be extended.
principles.example: Dieter Rams, 606 Universal Shelving System for Vitsœ, 1960

principles.name: Restraint
principles.idea: The product steps back so the user and their environment come forward.
principles.example: Hans Gugelot and Dieter Rams, Braun SK 4, 1956

movements.name: Saqqakhaneh
movements.summary: Iranian neo-traditional modernism that turned Shi'a votive objects, talismans, locks and script into modern painting, sculpture and graphic form.

principles.name: Folk-devotional objects as modern material
principles.idea: Locks, hands, talismans and astrolabes from water shrines become modern form.
principles.example: Parviz Tanavoli, Heech series, from the 1960s

principles.name: Script as visual matter
principles.idea: Letters are used for rhythm and charge rather than legibility.
principles.example: Hossein Zenderoudi, Who is this Hossein the world is crazy about?, linocut, 1958

principles.name: A grid of signs
principles.idea: Surfaces covered edge to edge with letters and numerals like a talisman.

movements.name: Expressive Typography (US)
movements.summary: Phototype freed display letters from metal, and New York art directors kerned, overlapped and scaled words until the word itself became the image.

principles.name: Typography as image
principles.idea: The word becomes the picture; meaning is expressed through the form of the letters.

principles.name: Tight, touching type
principles.idea: Phototype lets letters be kerned until they touch and overlap, forming new shapes.
principles.example: Herb Lubalin, Avant Garde magazine logotype, 1968

principles.name: Ligatures as expression
principles.idea: Alternates and ligatures are designed as the face's personality, not as exceptions.
principles.example: Herb Lubalin and Tom Carnase, ITC Avant Garde Gothic, 1970

principles.name: Type as architecture
principles.idea: Lettering at environmental scale turns a wall into a typographic composition.

principles.example: Morteza Momayez, ISIRI standards mark turning the initials into 'Iran', 1985

principles.name: One concentrated image
principles.idea: The poster states the film in a single image, partly learned from Polish posters.

principles.name: Children's culture as laboratory

principles.name: Calligraphy as structure
principles.idea: Letters enlarged and interlaced become architecture, not decoration.

principles.name: Script as the whole image

principles.name: Typography as the film's voice
principles.idea: The title is designed rather than illustrated; letterform carries mood.

movements.name: Cuban Poster
movements.summary: After 1959 Havana's film institute and solidarity organisation commissioned thousands of silkscreened and offset posters that sold cinema and revolution without selling products.

principles.name: A poster with nothing to sell
principles.idea: With advertising abolished, posters advertised films and causes, so designers could pursue metaphor and wit instead of product benefit.

movements.name: American Systems Modernism

movements.name: Mexico 68

movements.name: New Wave Typography
movements.summary: Swiss typography taken apart from inside: Weingart's Basel classroom kept the grid's discipline and broke its rules, and his students carried it to America.

principles.name: Break the grid from inside
principles.idea: Start from Swiss order, then stair-step, letterspace, rotate and overlap type so the structure is visible precisely because it is being violated.

principles.name: Film as a layer
principles.idea: Halftone screens, typesetting film and photographs are sandwiched and re-photographed, so texture and transparency become typographic material.

principles.name: Type in deep space
principles.idea: Letters, colour swatches and photographs float at different apparent depths, a layered space rather than a flat page.
principles.example: April Greiman and Jayme Odgers, CalArts poster, 1978

principles.name: Readability over legibility
principles.idea: Instead of maximising letter recognition, the designer asks whether the whole composition draws a reader in and holds them.
principles.example: Dan Friedman, teaching at Yale and SUNY Purchase, 1969-1975

movements.name: The GUI and the desktop metaphor
movements.summary: Windows, icons, menus and a pointer turned the computer into a picture of an office you could act on directly.

principles.name: Direct manipulation
principles.idea: Point at the thing and act on it, instead of typing a command that names it. The object on screen is the handle.
principles.example: Xerox Star 8010, drag a document icon onto the printer icon, 1981

principles.name: The metaphor as a teacher
principles.idea: Borrow a familiar world (desk, folder, trash) so a novice can predict what an action will do before trying it.
principles.example: Apple Macintosh Finder with folder and Trash icons, 1984

principles.name: What you see is what you get
principles.idea: The screen shows the printed result, so layout becomes something you see rather than something you encode.
principles.example: Gypsy editor on the Xerox Alto, Larry Tesler and Tim Mott, 1975

principles.name: Modelessness
principles.idea: The same gesture should mean the same thing everywhere; avoid hidden states that change what keys and clicks do.
principles.example: Cut, copy and paste as universal commands on the Apple Lisa, 1983

principles.name: Published consistency
principles.idea: Write the rules down so every application behaves alike; the guideline document is itself a design artefact.
principles.example: Human Interface Guidelines: The Apple Desktop Interface, 1987

movements.name: Computational design
movements.summary: Designers writing code as their material: type, layout and image generated by rules and responsive to data and time.

principles.name: Code is the material
principles.idea: The designer authors the rule that makes the form, not the form itself; changing a parameter is a design move.

principles.name: Type in space and time
principles.idea: Text is not fixed on a page but zooms, layers and moves through depth, with hierarchy expressed by distance and focus.
principles.example: Muriel Cooper and the Visible Language Workshop, Information Landscapes, TED5, 1994

principles.name: A sketchbook for programmers
principles.idea: Make the tool small and immediate enough that a designer sketches in code the way they sketch in pencil.
principles.example: Processing, Casey Reas and Ben Fry, 2001

principles.name: Rules plus chance
principles.idea: Compose with constrained randomness so each run yields a new but related image; the system is the signature.
principles.example: Joshua Davis, praystation.com, Prix Ars Electronica Golden Nica, 2001

movements.name: Punk and Post-punk Graphics
movements.summary: Cut-up, photocopied, deliberately crude graphics for the punk explosion, and the cool modernist sleeves of the post-punk labels that followed.

principles.name: Ransom-note lettering
principles.idea: Letters cut from newspaper headlines and pasted at mismatched sizes make the message look illicit and anonymous, made with scissors rather than a typesetter.
principles.example: Jamie Reid, 'God Save the Queen' sleeve for the Sex Pistols, 1977

principles.name: Détournement of icons
principles.idea: An official image is defaced just enough to invert its meaning: the Queen's jubilee portrait with the eyes and mouth torn out.
principles.example: Jamie Reid, 'God Save the Queen' poster, 1977

principles.name: The sleeve as a puzzle
principles.idea: Packaging carries deliberate errors, die-cuts, misregistration and hidden codes, so the object rewards close attention and insider knowledge.
principles.example: Barney Bubbles, Elvis Costello 'This Year's Model' sleeve, deliberately miscropped, 1978

principles.name: Modernism as a found object
principles.idea: Post-punk designers quote Tschichold, scientific plots and classical paintings with cool detachment, placing the band name small or not at all.

movements.name: Postmodern Typography
movements.summary: American and British designers read literary theory and the commercial vernacular into layouts that ask to be read in layers, not decoded once.

principles.name: Reading and seeing at once
principles.idea: Text is set to be both read and looked at: images and words interleave so meaning is assembled by the reader rather than delivered.
principles.example: Katherine McCoy, Cranbrook Graduate Program in Design poster, 1989

principles.name: Learn from the vernacular
principles.idea: Hand-lettered signs, clip art, Letraset and trade printing are treated as sources equal to Swiss modernism.
principles.example: Ed Fella, Detroit Focus Gallery poster 'Morris Brose: A Sustained Vision', 1987

principles.name: The designer as author
principles.idea: The designer adds a voice to the content rather than serving it invisibly, through self-initiated work, editing and commentary.
principles.example: Tibor Kalman, M&Co, Talking Heads '(Nothing But) Flowers' typographic video, 1988

principles.name: Theory as a design tool
principles.idea: Semiotics and post-structuralist ideas about how texts mean are tested directly in layout, and documented as a programme.
principles.example: Katherine and Michael McCoy, Cranbrook Design: The New Discourse, 1991

movements.name: Memphis
movements.summary: Sottsass's Milan collective made furniture out of cheap laminate, clashing colour and toy-like geometry to mock good taste and functionalist restraint.

principles.name: Cheap material, luxury price
principles.idea: Printed plastic laminate, the material of diners and kitchens, is applied to gallery furniture so status and taste are put in question.

principles.name: Pattern as surface, not ornament
principles.idea: A squiggle or speckle covers a form flatly and arbitrarily, unrelated to structure, making the surface a graphic layer.
principles.example: Ettore Sottsass, Bacterio laminate pattern, used on Memphis pieces from 1981

principles.name: Object as character
principles.idea: A bookcase or lamp is composed like a totem or a figure, with arms and a head, so it reads as personality before function.

principles.name: Clash on purpose
principles.idea: Colours and shapes that should not sit together are stacked: pastel with black, terrazzo with primary yellow.

movements.name: Japanese Emptiness
movements.summary: Muji's no-brand design grew into a philosophy of the empty vessel: design that offers space for meaning rather than pushing a message.

principles.name: The empty vessel
principles.idea: Design offers a space each person fills with their own meaning instead of transmitting a message.

principles.name: Subtract the brand
principles.idea: Remove logos, ornament and colour so material and price become the message.
principles.example: Ikko Tanaka, Muji launch packaging in kraft paper and cellophane, 1980

principles.name: White as potential
principles.idea: White is not absence but the state before content.

principles.name: Re-design the ordinary
principles.idea: Look again at everyday objects instead of inventing new ones.
principles.example: Kenya Hara, Re-Design: Daily Products of the 21st Century exhibition, 2000

principles.name: Clarity through organisation
principles.idea: Branding as tidying a client down to one essential form.
principles.example: Kashiwa Sato, Uniqlo identity for the SoHo New York flagship, 2006

movements.name: Emigre and Early Digital Type
movements.summary: A Berkeley magazine and foundry that designed type on and for the first Macintosh, then made the pages a public argument about legibility.

principles.name: Design for the machine's grain
principles.idea: Instead of forcing old typefaces into coarse screens and printers, letters are drawn from the pixel grid itself and its limits become the style.
principles.example: Zuzana Licko, Oakland (later Lo-Res), used in Emigre #3, 1985

principles.name: You read best what you read most
principles.idea: Legibility is learned habit, not a property of letterforms, so unfamiliar type is a question of exposure.

principles.name: The magazine as specimen
principles.idea: A publication shows its own foundry's fonts in use, and the fonts fund the magazine: medium, catalogue and business in one.
principles.example: Emigre magazine with Emigre Fonts, from 1985

principles.name: Distortion as a typeface
principles.idea: Typefaces encode accident, overlap and imperfection into the font file so any user can set 'damaged' type.
principles.example: Barry Deck, Template Gothic, drawn 1989, released by Emigre 1991

movements.name: Latin American Type Design
movements.summary: A continental type-design scene, from Buenos Aires typographic publishing to digital foundries and a regional biennial, selling Latin American letterforms to the world.

principles.name: A regional canon
principles.idea: A biennial that travels between countries builds a shared Latin American type culture rather than many national ones.

principles.name: Sell to the world from the periphery
principles.idea: Digital distribution lets a foundry outside the centres reach global brands directly.
principles.example: Latinotype, founded in Concepción, Chile, 2008; Trend among MyFonts' most popular fonts, 2013

principles.name: Signage as a national typeface practice
principles.idea: Large wayfinding commissions become the testing ground for custom lettering.
principles.example: Diseño Shakespear, Buenos Aires Subte signage, 1995-2008

movements.name: Grunge Typography
movements.summary: Layered, distressed, intuitive layouts made with QuarkXPress and Photoshop, where texture and attitude carried music and youth-culture content.

principles.name: Intuition over system
principles.idea: Each spread is composed by eye and mood, not from a master grid; consistency is in attitude, not in measurements.

principles.name: Text as image
principles.idea: Body copy is cropped, overlapped, set in dingbats or run off the page when its texture says more than its words.
principles.example: David Carson, Bryan Ferry interview set in Zapf Dingbats, Ray Gun, 1990s

principles.name: Corporate language turned on itself
principles.idea: Logos, slogans and manuals are parodied into an invented corporation's identity.
principles.example: The Designers Republic, packaging and identity for Wipeout, 1995

principles.name: Type with a grudge
principles.idea: Typefaces carry political names and historical baggage so their form and title argue with the reader.

images.title: Designers, Stay Away from Corporations billboard

movements.name: Early web and Web 1.0
movements.summary: Hypertext before stylesheets: default grey pages, tables hacked into grids, animated GIFs, and artists treating the browser itself as material.

principles.name: The link is the layout
principles.idea: Navigation is a web of blue underlined words; structure lives in the connections between pages, not on a single page.
principles.example: Tim Berners-Lee, first public website at CERN, 1991

principles.name: Image inline with text
principles.idea: Once pictures could sit inside the text flow, the page became a graphic surface rather than a document.

principles.name: Hack the medium
principles.idea: Coerce tools never meant for layout (tables, spacer GIFs, frames) into a grid; constraint becomes style.
principles.example: David Siegel, Creating Killer Web Sites, single-pixel GIF technique, 1996

principles.name: Vernacular authorship
principles.idea: Millions of amateurs publish with templates, counters, MIDI and under-construction signs; the amateur is the aesthetic.

principles.name: The browser as subject
principles.idea: Artists expose the machinery (frames, source code, errors) instead of hiding it.
principles.example: Olia Lialina, My Boyfriend Came Back from the War, 1996

movements.name: Y2K aesthetic
movements.summary: Translucent plastics, liquid chrome, blobs and techno-optimist sci-fi graphics around the millennium, revived by Gen Z in the 2020s.

principles.name: Translucency as candour
principles.idea: Show the insides through tinted plastic; the machine is friendly because you can see into it.
principles.example: Apple iMac G3 in Bondi Blue, 1998

principles.name: Liquid and chrome
principles.idea: Surfaces are glossy, reflective, bulbous, rendered rather than printed, signalling a digital future.
principles.example: Aqua interface preview at Macworld San Francisco, 2000

principles.name: Techno-graphic density
principles.idea: Layered pseudo-technical marks, codes and logotypes treat information graphics as decoration.
principles.example: The Designers Republic, Wipeout 2097 game graphics, 1996

movements.name: The Flash era
movements.summary: A vector plug-in let designers make the web move: intros, physics, generative toys and full-screen experiences outside HTML's limits.

principles.name: Motion as the primary medium
principles.idea: The site is a timeline; transitions, easing and choreography carry the brand more than static layout.

principles.name: Physics instead of buttons
principles.idea: Interface elements behave like springs, liquids and swarms, so interaction feels like handling a material.

principles.name: Open the source
principles.idea: Share the working files so the community learns by dissecting; the source is part of the work.
principles.example: Joshua Davis, praystation.com open FLA files, 2001

principles.name: Time as content
principles.idea: A loop that runs forever (a clock, a dance) becomes the experience itself and a reason to leave the page open.

movements.name: Neo-modernist Revival
movements.summary: Designers in Amsterdam and Zurich returned to grids, grotesques and black-and-white after grunge, treating modernism as a critical language, not a corporate one.

principles.name: Helvetica as a found material
principles.idea: A neutral grotesque is used without irony and without decoration, so meaning comes from scale, rhythm and repetition alone.
principles.example: Experimental Jetset, John & Paul & Ringo & George T-shirt, 2001

principles.name: The responsive identity
principles.idea: A mark is a system that changes shape to fit its context instead of a fixed logo.
principles.example: Experimental Jetset, Whitney Museum 'Responsive W' identity, 2013

principles.name: The book as architecture
principles.idea: Scale, thickness, edges and binding are designed as carefully as the pages, so the object itself carries the content.

principles.name: Construct the letter
principles.idea: Typefaces are rebuilt from first principles and rules, a modernist method producing deliberately odd results.

movements.name: Superflat
movements.summary: Murakami's theory that Japanese visual culture and postwar society are flat, run as a brand system spanning paintings, merchandise and luxury collaborations.

principles.name: Flatness as cultural theory
principles.idea: No perspective or depth: hard line and flat colour as a claim about a society, not only a style.
principles.example: Takashi Murakami, Superflat exhibition, Parco Gallery, 2000

principles.name: Collapse high and low
principles.idea: Paintings, figures, handbags and album covers treated as one practice.
principles.example: Murakami for Louis Vuitton, Multicolore monogram, 2003

principles.name: The character as brand
principles.idea: A mascot that mutates endlessly across media carries the identity.

principles.name: Cuteness carries trauma
principles.idea: Kawaii surfaces sit over the memory of defeat and the atomic bomb.
principles.example: Murakami, Little Boy exhibition, Japan Society, 2005

movements.name: Skeuomorphism
movements.summary: Interfaces rendered as physical things (gel buttons, leather, felt, wood, paper) to make new software feel familiar and touchable.

principles.name: Familiarity through imitation
principles.idea: Dress a new function in the look of the object it replaces so users already know how to read it.
principles.example: iOS Notes on a yellow legal pad, iPhone OS 1.0, 2007

principles.name: Light and material as hierarchy
principles.idea: Gloss, bevel and shadow say which things are pressable and which are background.
principles.example: Aqua gel buttons and pinstriped windows, Mac OS X 10.0, 2001

principles.name: Touch needs affordance
principles.idea: On a glass screen with no physical keys, rendered depth substitutes for touch feedback.
principles.example: iPhone slide-to-unlock with a rendered slider, 2007

principles.name: Craft as brand
principles.idea: Lavish rendering signals care and premium quality, especially for apps sold on a store.
principles.example: Apple Podcasts reel-to-reel tape deck, iOS 6, 2012

movements.name: Flat design
movements.summary: Ornament stripped out: solid colour, type-led hierarchy and the grid return, a direct import of Swiss modernism into software.

principles.name: Authentically digital
principles.idea: Stop imitating physical objects; let the screen be a screen, with type, colour and motion native to it.

principles.name: Content over chrome
principles.idea: Shrink or remove frames, bars and borders so the content is the interface.
principles.example: Windows Phone 7 panorama hubs with oversized Segoe headings bleeding off-screen, 2010

principles.name: Type as hierarchy
principles.idea: Scale and weight of a single sans-serif carry structure that bevels and boxes used to carry.

principles.name: Depth through layers, not texture
principles.idea: Translucent blurred panels and parallax give spatial order without rendering materials.

movements.name: Responsive web design
movements.summary: One layout that reflows across every screen using fluid grids, flexible images and media queries: the grid becomes a set of rules, not a fixed page.

principles.name: The fluid grid
principles.idea: Columns are proportions, not pixels; the grid stretches with the viewport.
principles.example: Ethan Marcotte, Responsive Web Design, A List Apart, 2010

principles.name: Breakpoints from content
principles.idea: Change the layout where the content breaks, not at named device widths.

principles.name: Mobile first
principles.idea: Design the narrowest, most constrained version first and enhance upward, which forces prioritisation.

principles.name: Intrinsic layout
principles.idea: Let elements size from their content with grid and flex rather than imposing a fixed column count.
principles.example: CSS Grid Layout shipping in major browsers, 2017

movements.name: Design systems
movements.summary: The corporate standards manual rebuilt as living code: tokens, components and documentation maintained by a team as a product.

principles.name: Systems, not pages
principles.idea: Design reusable components that compose into any page instead of designing pages one by one.
principles.example: Brad Frost, Atomic Design blog post, 2013

principles.name: Tokens as the single source
principles.idea: Colour, spacing and type become named variables shared by design tools and code, so a change propagates everywhere.

principles.name: The system is a product
principles.idea: A dedicated team versions, documents and supports the system, with adoption as its success metric.

principles.name: Defaults democratise
principles.idea: A free, good-enough kit lets non-designers ship coherent UI, at the cost of sameness.

principles.name: Shared canvas
principles.idea: Libraries live in a multiplayer design tool so the source of truth is collaborative and in the browser.

movements.name: Material Design
movements.summary: Google's system of paper-like surfaces with real shadows and meaningful motion, later personalised (Material You, 2021) and made more emotional (Expressive, 2025).

principles.name: Material is the metaphor
principles.idea: A single invented physical material (sheets of paper with thickness) gives consistent rules for depth, shadow and stacking without imitating any real object.

principles.name: Motion provides meaning
principles.idea: Transitions show where things came from and where they went; animation is explanation, not decoration.
principles.example: Android 5.0 Lollipop ripple and shared-element transitions, 2014

principles.name: Bold, graphic, intentional
principles.idea: Print-design grids, baseline, scale and saturated colour drive hierarchy.
principles.example: Material Design 2014 spec with 8dp grid and Roboto type scale

principles.name: Personal by default
principles.idea: Colour is extracted from the user's wallpaper so the system adapts to the person, not the brand.

principles.name: Expressive and tested
principles.idea: Shape, size, colour and springy motion are dialled up to evoke emotion, with each choice validated by research.
principles.example: Material 3 Expressive, 46 studies with over 18,000 participants, 2025

movements.name: Neubrutalism
movements.summary: A deliberate roughness against polished system UI: thick black outlines, hard offset shadows, flat clashing colour and visible structure.

principles.name: Show the structure
principles.idea: Borders, boxes and the grid are drawn, not hidden; the page admits it is made of rectangles.

principles.name: Hard shadow, no blur
principles.idea: Depth is a solid offset block (often black, a few pixels down-right), a printmaker's shadow rather than a renderer's.
principles.example: Neobrutalist UI patterns surveyed by NN/g, 2025

principles.name: Clash on purpose
principles.idea: Two or three saturated flat colours against black and white, chosen to be loud rather than harmonious.
principles.example: Gumroad storefront and dashboard, cited by NN/g, 2025

principles.name: Anti-polish as voice
principles.idea: Roughness signals independence from big-tech sameness and suits creator and indie brands.
principles.example: Figma brand refresh, cited by NN/g, 2025

movements.name: Generative AI design
movements.summary: Images, interfaces and code produced from natural-language prompts; the designer shifts from making artefacts to directing, curating and constraining a model.

principles.name: Describe, then select
principles.idea: The designer writes intent in words and curates among many outputs; taste and editing replace drawing as the core act.
principles.example: Midjourney open beta via Discord, July 2022

principles.name: Conversation as interface
principles.idea: A text box and a thread replace menus; the command line returns, but in natural language.

principles.name: Latent style
principles.idea: Every historical style is addressable by name, so pastiche is instant and originality must come from the brief and the edit.
principles.example: Jason Allen, Théâtre D'opéra Spatial, made with Midjourney, Colorado State Fair, 2022

principles.name: Prompt to product
principles.idea: Working interfaces and code are generated from a description and refined by feedback, collapsing design and build.

principles.name: The system constrains the model
principles.idea: Design systems become the guardrails (tokens, components) that keep generated UI on-brand and usable.

movements.name: Liquid Glass
movements.summary: Apple's 2025 cross-platform material: real-time refracting, reflecting translucent controls floating over content, praised as craft and criticised for legibility.

principles.name: A digital material
principles.idea: Controls are made of one simulated substance with optical behaviour (lensing, specular highlights) rendered live by the GPU.

principles.name: Controls float above content
principles.idea: Navigation is a separate functional layer of floating capsules that shrink on scroll, rather than bars pinned to the screen edge.
principles.example: iOS 26 tab bar that collapses while scrolling in Apple Music, 2025

principles.name: Concentricity
principles.idea: Corner radii of controls nest inside the radii of windows and the hardware itself, so software echoes the device's shape.

principles.name: One language across devices
principles.idea: The same material and rules span phone, tablet, desktop, watch, TV and headset.
principles.example: iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26, watchOS 26, tvOS 26, visionOS 26, 2025

figures.name: Owen Jones
figures.role: Architect, ornament theorist, chromolithographic book designer
figures.summary: His Grammar of Ornament turned the world's decoration into a teachable system of propositions and brought chromolithography to its peak.

principles.name: Ornament has rules
principles.idea: Decoration follows stated propositions about geometry, proportion and colour, so it can be taught rather than merely copied.
principles.example: The Grammar of Ornament, 37 general propositions, 1856

principles.name: Decorate construction
principles.idea: Ornament should grow from and clarify the structure of the object, never be built for its own sake.

principles.name: Flat for flat surfaces
principles.idea: Ornament on a flat surface should be flat and conventionalised, not a naturalistic illusion of depth.
principles.example: Plates of stylised leaves and flowers in The Grammar of Ornament, 1856

figures.name: Walter Crane
figures.summary: Crane's colour toy books with printer Edmund Evans made the picture book a designed object, and his later teaching codified Arts and Crafts design.

principles.name: The page as decorative unit
principles.idea: Picture, border and text are composed together as one flat decorative panel.

principles.name: Line first
principles.idea: Outline is the fundamental means of design; colour and mass come second.

principles.name: Design for the press
principles.idea: Draw for the limits of the reproduction method, here a few flat colour blocks, rather than against them.
principles.example: Toy books engraved and printed by Edmund Evans, 1865-1876

figures.name: Eugène Grasset
figures.role: Illustrator, poster artist, type designer, teacher of ornament
figures.summary: Grasset joined medieval line and Japanese flatness, designed a typeface, and wrote the method books that taught a generation of French ornament.

principles.name: Text and image in one plate
principles.idea: Illustration, border and text are printed together and interpenetrate on every page of the book.

principles.name: Contour and flat fill
principles.idea: A thick, even outline encloses flat colour, a stained-glass logic adapted to lithography.

principles.name: Ornament from the plant
principles.idea: Study a real plant's structure, then derive borders and motifs from it methodically.
principles.example: La Plante et ses applications ornementales, 1896

keyWorks.title: Salon des Cent: Exposition E. Grasset

figures.name: Jules Chéret
figures.summary: The father of the modern poster: Chéret industrialised the large colour lithograph and invented the joyful poster heroine Paris called the Chérette.

principles.name: Three stones, maximum colour
principles.idea: Build the image from a few overlapping colour stones, typically red, yellow and blue over a black key, to get rich colour cheaply.

principles.name: Movement as message
principles.idea: A single figure caught mid-leap or mid-spin carries the energy of the product; the event sells itself through motion.

principles.name: Letters that float
principles.idea: Hand-drawn lettering curves around the figure and into the air, integrated with the image rather than set in a separate band.

figures.name: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec
figures.summary: In about thirty posters Lautrec brought Japanese flatness, cropping and caricature to the Paris wall, and made a person into a graphic sign.

principles.name: The silhouette as character
principles.idea: Reduce a person to one unmistakable flat shape: a hat, a scarf, a black glove.

principles.name: Layered planes
principles.idea: Stack a cropped foreground shape, a midground subject and a flat background to create space with no perspective drawing.

principles.name: Spatter as tone
principles.idea: Crachis, ink spattered from a toothbrush across the stone, gives texture and half-tone without hatching.

figures.name: Alphonse Mucha
figures.summary: Mucha's Bernhardt posters and decorative panels fixed the Art Nouveau formula: a woman, a halo, swirling hair and a Byzantine frame.

principles.name: The template
principles.idea: A repeatable layout of figure, circular halo, mosaic arch and lettering band could be refilled for any client.
principles.example: Gismonda, 1894; repeated across the Bernhardt posters to 1899

principles.name: The tall format
principles.idea: An extreme vertical, near life-size sheet turns the figure into a standing presence on the street.

principles.name: A pattern book for the style
principles.idea: Publish the system itself as plates so others can apply it to any object.

figures.name: Aubrey Beardsley
figures.summary: In six years Beardsley made black-and-white line work as graphic and as transgressive as anything in the period, drawn for the new photo-engraved line block.

principles.name: Black and white, nothing between
principles.idea: Pure black masses against pure white paper with no grey, so the image survives cheap photomechanical line-block reproduction.

principles.name: Line against mass
principles.idea: Hairline detail is set against huge flat black areas so each makes the other louder.

principles.name: The cover as a brand
principles.idea: A bold, flat cover image gives a periodical an unmistakable face on the bookstall.

images.title: Le Morte d'Arthur: How Morgan le Fay Gave a Shield to Sir Tristram

figures.name: The Beggarstaffs
figures.role: Poster design partnership of James Pryde (1866-1941) and William Nicholson (1872-1949)
figures.summary: Pryde and Nicholson cut posters from flat paper shapes and let the viewer's eye complete them, a reduction a decade ahead of Plakatstil.

principles.name: Collage of flat shapes
principles.idea: Compose by cutting and arranging pieces of coloured paper, then print the result as flat colour.

principles.name: Let the eye close the shape
principles.idea: Leave out contours where figure and ground share a colour, so the image completes itself in the viewer's head.

principles.name: Two colours and a big shape
principles.idea: Use a very few flat colours and one dominant silhouette sized for the hoarding.

figures.name: Will Bradley
figures.summary: America's first great designer-typographer: Bradley adapted Beardsley's line into posters and covers, then ran his own press and type revivals.

principles.name: Repeat for rhythm
principles.idea: Duplicate or mirror a figure to make a flat, rhythmic pattern from a single drawing.

principles.name: Type and drawing share weight
principles.idea: Hand lettering and the drawing use the same weight of black, so they fuse into one block.

principles.name: Look backward to move forward
principles.idea: Revive colonial American chapbook typography, Caslon and woodcut ornament, as a fresh vernacular.

figures.name: Margaret Macdonald
figures.role: Artist, designer, member of The Four
figures.summary: Macdonald co-authored the Glasgow Style's ghostly figures and rose motifs, in posters and gesso panels that were among the first statements of it.

principles.name: The emblematic figure
principles.idea: Attenuated, symmetrical figures function as signs rather than portraits, almost lettering in themselves.
principles.example: Glasgow Institute of the Fine Arts poster, with Frances Macdonald and Herbert MacNair, 1895

principles.name: Surface as relief
principles.idea: Gesso, string, beads and metal leaf build a low relief that catches light like a printed varnish.

figures.name: William Morris
figures.summary: Morris made design a moral project, built a firm that made what it designed, and with the Kelmscott Press restarted serious book typography.

principles.name: Useful or beautiful
principles.idea: Nothing belongs in a home unless it is known to be useful or believed to be beautiful; the test applies to every object.

principles.name: Structure under pattern
principles.idea: Every repeat is built on a hidden armature, a diagonal trellis or a turnover, so dense ornament stays legible.

principles.name: Return to the source
principles.idea: When a craft has decayed, go back to its best historical moment and relearn it by doing, from dye vat to punch.
principles.example: Golden Type, modelled on Nicolas Jenson's roman of 1470, 1890

principles.name: The book as a whole
principles.idea: Type, paper, ink, margins, initials and borders are designed together as a single object.
principles.example: The Works of Geoffrey Chaucer, Kelmscott Press, 1896
