figures.name: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
figures.summary: Mackintosh joined Art Nouveau's organic line to a rectilinear grid, and his elongated posters and total interiors helped turn Vienna square.

principles.name: The vertical stretch
principles.idea: Elongate everything, figures, chair backs and lettering, until it reads as an architectural column.

principles.name: Square and rose
principles.idea: Pair a hard grid of small squares with a single soft organic motif; the contrast is the style.

principles.name: Light and dark rooms
principles.idea: Design environments in white or dark keys, with colour reserved for tiny accents of mauve or pink.

images.title: Willow Tea Rooms: Room de Luxe

figures.name: Gustav Klimt
figures.role: Painter, Secession founder and first president, poster designer
figures.summary: The Secession's first president, Klimt brought gold, flat pattern and a radically empty layout to its first poster and its exhibitions.

principles.name: The empty middle
principles.idea: Leave the centre of the sheet blank and push image and text to the edges, so the void becomes the event.

principles.name: Pattern as space
principles.idea: Flat ornamental fields of gold, spirals and squares replace perspective and surround naturalistic faces and hands.

figures.name: Koloman Moser
figures.role: Graphic designer, Secession and Wiener Werkstätte co-founder
figures.summary: Moser was the Secession's chief graphic designer: Ver Sacrum, block lettering, modular pattern and Austria's stamps and banknotes.

principles.name: Letters as building blocks
principles.idea: Draw letters as condensed rectangles that lock together into a solid field of type.

principles.name: Pattern by module
principles.idea: Generate ornament by repeating and rotating a simple unit on a grid, so the method is visible.

principles.name: The state as client
principles.idea: Apply the modern style to official, mass-circulation graphics such as postage and currency.

keyWorks.title: Wiener Werkstätte marks and stationery (with Josef Hoffmann)

figures.name: Henry van de Velde
figures.summary: Van de Velde pushed Art Nouveau into pure abstract line and founded the Weimar school that the Bauhaus grew from.

principles.name: Abstract line as force
principles.idea: Line carries energy and emotion by itself, with no flowers or figures required.

principles.name: The artist's individuality
principles.idea: Defended the designer's free invention against standardised types in the 1914 Werkbund debate with Hermann Muthesius.

figures.name: Otto Eckmann
figures.role: Painter turned graphic and type designer
figures.summary: Eckmann gave up painting for applied design and drew the defining Jugendstil typeface, a brush-written letter that fused type with ornament.

principles.name: Type from the brush
principles.idea: Letters are written with a broad brush, so the swell and taper of the stroke matches the plant ornament around them.

principles.name: Applied over fine
principles.idea: Treat the magazine cover and the typeface as the serious work, ahead of the easel picture.
principles.example: Auctioned his paintings to work on Pan and Jugend, 1894-1896

figures.name: Josef Hoffmann
figures.summary: Nicknamed Quadratl-Hoffmann for his squares, he made the grid a total design language from cutlery to the Palais Stoclet.

principles.name: The square everywhere
principles.idea: One module, the square, at every scale from a perforated basket to a facade, gives an entire environment one voice.

principles.name: Better ten days on one thing
principles.idea: Quality of making is the brand: the workshop prefers slow, excellent production to fast, mediocre volume.

principles.name: Contour as frame
principles.idea: Outline edges in a contrasting band, like a dark metal trim on white stone, so form reads as drawing.

figures.name: Lucian Bernhard
figures.summary: Bernhard's Priester matches poster, two matches and a word, founded the Sachplakat and the idea that a brand is a product and a name.

principles.name: Subtract until it breaks
principles.idea: Remove every element that is not the product or its name, then check the poster still works from across the street.

principles.name: The name as the hero
principles.idea: The brand name, in heavy hand-drawn sans or Fraktur-derived capitals, is given equal visual weight to the object.

principles.name: Contrasting fields
principles.idea: Set the object and lettering on a dark, flat ground with one hot accent colour.

figures.name: Peter Behrens
figures.summary: From Jugendstil woodcuts to AEG's artistic consultant, Behrens designed a company's buildings, products, type and print as one: the first corporate identity.

principles.name: One hand for everything
principles.idea: The same designer shapes the factory, the kettle, the catalogue, the typeface and the trademark, so the company has one face.

principles.name: Geometry over ornament
principles.idea: Replace naturalistic decoration with a modular grid and simple geometric marks.

principles.name: Type standards
principles.idea: Draw a house typeface and use it consistently, so the letters themselves identify the company.

principles.name: Standardised parts, varied products
principles.idea: Combine a small set of interchangeable components into a product range.

figures.name: F.T. Marinetti
figures.summary: Founded Futurism with a 1909 newspaper manifesto and invented words-in-freedom, typography that behaves like noise.

principles.name: Words-in-freedom
principles.idea: Abolish syntax, adjectives and punctuation; let nouns collide on the page.

principles.name: The manifesto as medium
principles.idea: A movement exists once it has published its rules in public.
principles.example: Manifesto of Futurism, Le Figaro front page, 1909

principles.name: Typographic dissonance
principles.idea: The page should break typographic harmony on purpose.

figures.name: Ludwig Hohlwein
figures.summary: Munich's master of the figure poster, Hohlwein built people from flat patches of light and shade; his later work served Nazi propaganda.

principles.name: Light as flat shapes
principles.idea: Break a figure into interlocking flat zones of light and shadow, so it reads as volume with no modelling.

principles.name: Texture against flatness
principles.idea: Set a patterned area, a check or a stipple, against plain fields to give a flat poster tactile richness.

figures.name: Wyndham Lewis
figures.summary: Founded Vorticism and wrote most of BLAST, whose magenta cover and slabs of grotesque type made polemic into layout.

principles.name: Polemic as layout
principles.idea: The argument is carried by type scale and list structure.

principles.name: Hard edges over speed lines
principles.idea: Static mechanical structure rather than Futurist blur.

figures.name: Kazimir Malevich
figures.nationality: Russian (born in Kyiv, of Polish descent)
figures.summary: Founded Suprematism with Black Square in 1915 and taught a grammar of pure geometric form at Vitebsk.

principles.name: Feeling over object
principles.idea: Art should give pure sensation, not depict things.

principles.name: Reduction as a radical act
principles.idea: The smallest possible statement is the most provocative.

principles.name: Teach the elements
principles.idea: A vocabulary of forms can be transmitted as a school.

keyWorks.title: From Cubism and Futurism to Suprematism

figures.name: Hugo Ball
figures.role: Poet, performer, co-founder of the Cabaret Voltaire
figures.summary: Opened the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in 1916 and pioneered sound poetry, language heard below meaning.

principles.name: Language below meaning
principles.idea: Invented words heard as pure sound.

principles.name: The body as typeface
principles.idea: Performance and costume as composition.
principles.example: Cardboard costume for the sound poems, Cabaret Voltaire, 1916

figures.name: Theo van Doesburg
figures.role: Painter, writer, designer, editor of De Stijl
figures.summary: Founded and edited De Stijl, carried it into the Bauhaus, and tilted its grid into Elementarism's diagonal.

principles.name: The magazine as movement
principles.idea: An editor's consistent format can become a school.

principles.name: Construct the alphabet
principles.idea: Letters as modular rectangles.

principles.name: Dynamism through the diagonal
principles.idea: Tilt the orthogonal grid 45 degrees.

figures.name: Ernst Keller
figures.summary: The teacher behind the Swiss school: from 1918 his Zürich course made analysis of the problem the starting point of every design.

principles.name: The problem determines the form
principles.idea: Derive the solution from content and brief, not from a house style.
principles.example: Graphic design course, Kunstgewerbeschule Zürich, from 1918

principles.name: Lettering as architecture
principles.idea: Type treated as a constructed, monumental object.

principles.name: Simple geometry, intense colour
principles.idea: Bold simplified shapes and strong flat colour carry the message.

figures.name: Hannah Höch
figures.summary: Berlin Dada's only woman and a co-inventor of photomontage, using the illustrated press to dissect power and gender.

principles.name: Collage as social X-ray
principles.idea: Scale and juxtaposition expose power.

principles.name: Gender as subject
principles.idea: The press's New Woman, re-cut and questioned.

principles.name: Craft pattern as source
principles.idea: Domestic templates meet magazine photography.

figures.name: El Lissitzky
figures.role: Artist, architect, book and exhibition designer
figures.summary: Carried Suprematism into books, posters and exhibitions, and carried the Russian avant-garde to Berlin, Hanover and the Bauhaus.

principles.name: Optics over phonetics
principles.idea: The printed word is learnt by sight, so design for the eye.

principles.name: The book as constructed object
principles.idea: Sequence, index and spread designed like a building.
principles.example: Dlia golosa, with die-cut thumb index, 1923

principles.name: Abstract narrative
principles.idea: Geometric forms can tell a story.

principles.name: Exhibition as immersive medium
principles.idea: The display space itself is the message.

keyWorks.title: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge

images.title: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge

figures.name: Walter Gropius
figures.summary: Founded and directed the Bauhaus, designing the school itself as the work, then carried it to Harvard.

principles.name: The school as a design
principles.idea: A curriculum is a designed system that shapes everyone in it.

principles.name: Art and technology, a new unity
principles.idea: Artists should design for industrial production.

principles.name: Building as the total work
principles.idea: Every workshop contributes to one object.

figures.name: Edward McKnight Kauffer
figures.summary: American in London who brought Vorticist and Cubist form to about 140 London Underground posters and to Shell.

principles.name: Avant-garde form for a public client
principles.idea: Abstraction used to sell newspapers and travel.
principles.example: Soaring to Success! Daily Herald – the Early Bird, 1918–1919

principles.name: Many styles, one patron
principles.idea: The client's system holds the identity while the idiom changes.

principles.name: Abstract symbol for an abstract service
principles.idea: Invisible infrastructure shown as a symbolic image.
principles.example: Power, the Nerve Centre of London's Underground, 1930

figures.name: Kurt Schwitters
figures.summary: Built Merz from found fragments and proved Dada play and Constructivist order could share a page and an ad agency.

principles.name: Build from fragments
principles.idea: Everything had broken; new work is made from the pieces.

principles.name: Play and order together
principles.idea: Dada and Constructivism are compatible on one page.
principles.example: Merz 4, carrying Lissitzky's Topography of Typography, 1923

principles.name: Typography as illustration
principles.idea: Letters, rules and bars act as characters.
principles.example: Die Scheuche, with Käte Steinitz and Theo van Doesburg, 1925

figures.name: Joost Schmidt
figures.summary: Designed the 1923 Bauhaus exhibition poster and ran the school's advertising and printing department from 1928 to 1932.

principles.name: Geometry as composition
principles.idea: Circles, squares and rules interlocked like machine parts.

principles.name: Teach advertising as a system
principles.idea: Typography, photography and exhibition design as one curriculum.

figures.name: Alexander Rodchenko
figures.summary: Gave up painting for posters, books and photography, fusing slogan, photograph and bold type into one Constructivist shout.

principles.name: Image and word as one shout
principles.idea: Photograph, slogan and type locked into a single structure, made with the copywriter.

principles.name: Photography as the new drawing
principles.idea: Montaged photographs replace illustration.

principles.name: The radical viewpoint
principles.idea: Steep diagonal up- and down-shots make the familiar strange.

figures.name: Varvara Stepanova
figures.summary: Constructivist who carried geometric design into textiles, sportswear and stage design for mass production.

principles.name: Pattern from production
principles.idea: Geometric prints designed for the machine and the worker.
principles.example: Textile designs for the First State Textile Printing Factory, 1924

principles.name: Clothes as working tools
principles.idea: Sports and work clothing designed for function and legibility.

principles.name: Visual poetry by hand
principles.idea: Handwritten word-and-image books.

keyWorks.title: The Death of Tarelkin (sets and costumes)

figures.name: László Moholy-Nagy
figures.summary: Brought Constructivism to the Bauhaus, coined typophoto and the New Vision, and founded the New Bauhaus in Chicago.

principles.name: Typophoto
principles.idea: Typography plus photography is the most exact visual communication.

principles.name: The New Vision
principles.idea: Camera, microscope and X-ray extend human seeing.

principles.name: Communication first
principles.idea: Typography must achieve absolute clarity before anything else.
principles.example: Die neue Typographie essay, Staatliches Bauhaus in Weimar 1919–1923, 1923

figures.name: Herbert Bayer
figures.summary: Ran the Bauhaus print workshop, proposed a single lowercase alphabet, and carried Bauhaus rigour into American corporate design.

principles.name: One alphabet
principles.idea: Abolish capitals; a single geometric lowercase is enough.

principles.name: Hierarchy without decoration
principles.idea: Order comes from weight, size and rule alone.

principles.name: Photography as the designer's tool
principles.idea: The designer's own photograph becomes the cover.

figures.name: Karel Teige
figures.summary: Leader and theorist of Devětsil and Poetism whose book typography and photomontage made the Czech avant-garde a typographic movement.

principles.name: Typography as poetry's second voice
principles.idea: The layout carries the poem's meaning, not just its text.

principles.name: Montage over illustration
principles.idea: Photographs are cut and recombined into a new statement.

principles.name: Function as a social programme
principles.idea: Design as the scientific solution of exact tasks of rational construction.

figures.name: Fortunato Depero
figures.summary: Futurist who made the portfolio a bolted object and built Campari's entire visual world, down to the bottle.

principles.name: Self-promotion as a format
principles.idea: The portfolio is itself a designed object.

principles.name: Brand as a total world
principles.idea: Ads, objects and packaging speak one invented language.

principles.name: Mechanical figuration
principles.idea: People and things reduced to toy-like interlocking solids.

figures.name: Paul Renner
figures.summary: Designed Futura, the geometric sans marketed as the typeface of our time, and ran Munich's master school for printers.

principles.name: Geometry corrected by the eye
principles.idea: Start from circle, triangle and square, then adjust optically so the type reads.

principles.name: Type for the age
principles.idea: A typeface can be a manifesto for its period.
principles.example: Bauer's Futura slogan, die Schrift unserer Zeit, 1927

principles.name: Printing as design education
principles.idea: Train printers as designers.
principles.example: Meisterschule für Deutschlands Buchdrucker, Munich, from 1927

figures.name: Qian Juntao
figures.role: Book cover designer, seal carver, calligrapher
figures.summary: Kaiming Bookstore's art editor (1927-1934), nicknamed 'Qian Covers', who made cover design a recognised craft in Republican Shanghai.

principles.name: The seal carver's economy
principles.idea: A carved seal's compression, few strokes in a square field, brought to the cover.

principles.name: Western pattern, Chinese structure
principles.idea: Art Nouveau and Deco ornament for borders and grounds while titles stay hand-drawn Chinese characters.

figures.name: Jan Tschichold
figures.summary: Codified the avant-garde into the rules of Die neue Typographie, then recanted and standardised Penguin Books.

principles.name: Codify for the trade
principles.idea: Make radical form a standard ordinary compositors can follow.

principles.name: Functional asymmetry
principles.idea: Arrange by reading order and importance, not a central axis.

principles.name: Rules, then judgment
principles.idea: Apply the same rigour to classical books when the context changes.

figures.name: Piet Zwart
figures.summary: Self-styled typotekt who made a cable company's catalogue into an avant-garde object with stock type and overprinted photography.

principles.name: Build with the printer's case
principles.idea: Compose from stock type, rules and blanks.

principles.name: Photography as fact
principles.idea: Close-up, cropped, overprinted product photographs.

principles.name: Play inside a functional brief
principles.idea: A public-service manual can be joyful.

figures.name: Zhang Guangyu
figures.summary: Led Shanghai's manhua golden age through Shanghai Sketch and Modern Sketch, fusing Deco, Constructivism and folk art; later designed Havoc in Heaven.

principles.name: Synthesis without hierarchy
principles.idea: Bauhaus, Constructivism, Mexican murals and Chinese folk art in one decorative language.

principles.name: Myth as political weapon
principles.idea: Classical stories retold to satirise the present.
principles.example: Journey to the West caricature cycle, 1945

principles.name: Design across every medium
principles.idea: Furniture, covers, stamps and film from one hand.

figures.name: Stenberg Brothers (Vladimir & Georgii Stenberg)
figures.summary: Vladimir (1899–1982) and Georgii (1900–1933) made around 300 film posters that brought cinema's cuts and angles to lithography.

principles.name: Stop the passer-by
principles.idea: Distortion, inversion and scale arrest people in motion.

principles.name: Hand-drawn photography
principles.idea: Film stills redrawn so montage effects print in flat lithographic colour.
principles.example: Berlin: Symphony of a Great City, 1928

principles.name: Cinema's rhythm in a still
principles.idea: Repeated, rotating figures suggest editing.

keyWorks.title: Berlin: Symphony of a Great City

figures.name: Piet Mondrian
figures.summary: Reduced painting to black bars and primary rectangles in dynamic equilibrium, the grid's most quoted ancestor.

principles.name: Dynamic equilibrium
principles.idea: Unequal rectangles held in asymmetric balance.
principles.example: Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow, 1930

principles.name: Line as structure
principles.idea: Black bars of varied weight divide the field rather than outline objects.
principles.example: Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow, 1930

principles.name: Rhythm from a grid
principles.idea: Repetition and interval as music.

figures.name: Gustav Klutsis
figures.summary: Made photomontage monumental in Soviet posters with Valentina Kulagina, then was executed in Stalin's purges in 1938.

principles.name: Photomontage at monumental scale
principles.idea: Repeated photographed figures become a mass.
principles.example: Let Us Fulfill the Plan of Great Works, 1930

principles.name: Montage plus geometry
principles.idea: Suprematist planes structure the photographs.

principles.name: Multimedia street furniture
principles.idea: Kiosks combining screen, loudspeaker and print.

figures.name: Otto Neurath
figures.summary: Vienna Circle philosopher who invented the Vienna Method, later Isotype, to give working people statistics in pictures.

principles.name: Visual education as democracy
principles.idea: Social data belongs to the people it describes, so it must be readable by them.
principles.example: Gesellschafts- und Wirtschaftsmuseum exhibitions, Vienna, from 1925

principles.name: A grammar for pictures
principles.idea: Rules for combining signs, like a language.

figures.name: Marie Neurath
figures.summary: Isotype's principal transformer, who decided what each chart should say, named the method and ran it for 26 years after Otto.

principles.name: The transformer
principles.idea: A role between expert and artist that decides what a chart should say before it is drawn.

principles.name: Information for new readers
principles.idea: Design for children and new citizens first.
principles.example: Isotype Institute voter education material for Western Nigeria, 1950s

figures.name: Gerd Arntz
figures.nationality: German (worked in Austria and the Netherlands)
figures.summary: Woodcut artist who drew Isotype's roughly 4,000 pictograms, the ancestors of every icon set and signage system.

principles.name: Reduce to a type
principles.idea: Each pictogram is the type of a thing, not a portrait of one.

principles.name: Woodcut economy
principles.idea: Silhouette and minimal interior detail, cut for reproduction.

figures.name: John Heartfield
figures.summary: Turned Dada photomontage into anti-Nazi weaponry on the covers of the communist AIZ, one seamless image per idea.

principles.name: Make the photograph tell the truth
principles.idea: Seamless montage gives satire the authority of documentary.
principles.example: Adolf, the Superman: Swallows Gold and Spouts Junk, AIZ, 1932

principles.name: One image, one idea
principles.idea: A single sharp visual pun locked by a caption.
principles.example: Four axes forming a swastika, AIZ, 1934

principles.name: The jacket as poster
principles.idea: The book cover argues the book's politics.

figures.name: Herbert Matter
figures.summary: Swiss photomontage pioneer who brought scale collision to America and built Knoll's identity almost entirely out of how its furniture was photographed.

principles.name: Scale collision
principles.idea: A huge close-up beside a tiny figure makes the image deep before a word is read.

principles.name: The product as abstract sculpture
principles.idea: Furniture is photographed as form, shadow and line with almost no copy.

principles.name: One sign for a whole system
principles.idea: A single monogram applied to everything from vehicles to timetables.

figures.name: A.M. Cassandre
figures.summary: The great Art Deco poster artist: one geometric image for viewers in motion, with type built into the picture.

principles.name: The poster as telegram
principles.idea: One simple image read at speed from a car or train.

principles.name: Image and type from one geometry
principles.idea: Display letters drawn from the same forms as the picture.

principles.name: Serial motion
principles.idea: A sequence of frames tells the story to a moving viewer.

principles.name: Monumental viewpoint
principles.idea: Low angle and extreme scale make the product heroic.

figures.name: Lester Beall
figures.summary: Among the first American-born modernists; his Rural Electrification posters turned Constructivist arrows and stripes into a public American language.

principles.name: Graphic signs over illustration
principles.idea: Arrows, stripes and flat flags persuade more directly than a painted scene.

principles.name: Photomontage for the common good
principles.idea: Documentary photographs of real people, cut out against flat colour, sell a public programme.

principles.name: Codify the mark
principles.idea: An identity is written into a standards manual so it outlives its designer.

figures.name: Hiromu Hara
figures.summary: Brought the New Typography to Japan, art-directed FRONT, co-founded the Nippon Design Center and lettered the Tokyo 1964 emblem.

principles.name: Typography serves the client
principles.idea: Designs built logically, without a signature style, on the client's side.

principles.name: Paper is part of the design
principles.idea: The substrate is designed, not picked from stock.
principles.example: Paper series developed with Takeo, from 1959

principles.name: Modern means, any message
principles.idea: His wartime FRONT shows the New Typography serving propaganda: form does not carry ethics.

figures.name: Leopoldo Méndez
figures.role: Printmaker, co-founder of the Taller de Gráfica Popular
figures.summary: Mexico's central political printmaker, heir to Posada, who co-founded the TGP in 1937 and later cut prints for Mexican cinema.

principles.name: Anonymity in the service of the message
principles.idea: He kept individual credit small and worked through collectives, treating authorship as less important than reach.

principles.name: The print as cinema
principles.idea: Sequences of prints work like film stills, and prints can enter film itself.
principles.example: Engravings for Emilio Fernández's Río Escondido, late 1940s

principles.name: Posada's line, modern politics
principles.idea: The popular broadside's directness is used for anti-fascism and labour, not just satire.

keyWorks.title: Illustrations for Incidentes melódicos del mundo irracional
Engraved mural dedicated to José Guadalupe Posada, Talleres Gráficos de la Nación

figures.name: Alvin Lustig
figures.role: Book designer, graphic and interior designer
figures.summary: Made the New Directions paperback a site of modern art with abstract, symbolic jackets, and argued the designer should be a generalist.

principles.name: Symbol, not illustration
principles.idea: A jacket evokes the spirit of the text with an abstract sign rather than depicting a scene.

principles.name: The designer as total designer
principles.idea: One designer moves across books, interiors, furniture and type.

principles.name: Modern art as vernacular
principles.idea: Lessons from Miró, Klee and Surrealism reach a mass audience on a cheap cover.
principles.example: A Streetcar Named Desire jacket, New Directions, 1947

images.title: Nausea, New Classics
images.credit: Karen Horton, diseño de la cubierta de Alvin Lustig, The New Classics Series pub

figures.name: Cipe Pineles
figures.summary: First woman to art-direct major American mass-market magazines; at Seventeen and Charm she brought fine artists and real women's lives onto the page.

principles.name: Fine art in mass media
principles.idea: Commission serious painters, not illustrators, to interpret fiction.
principles.example: Seventeen, with art by Ben Shahn, Ad Reinhardt and Andy Warhol, 1947–50

principles.name: Design for the reader's real life
principles.idea: Fashion shown in offices and streets for women who work.

principles.name: The hand as voice
principles.idea: Painted, hand-lettered illustration warms photographic glamour.
principles.example: Leave Me Alone with the Recipes, made 1940s, published 2017

figures.name: Nasri Khattar
figures.summary: Lebanese architect who devised Unified Arabic, a one-form-per-letter printing script of 33 glyphs (patented 1947, launched 1957).

principles.name: Rationalise the system, not the letter
principles.idea: Combine isolated and connected features so each letter needs one form.

principles.name: For print only
principles.idea: Handwriting stays; the reform is for the machine.

figures.name: Giovanni Pintori
figures.summary: Olivetti's advertising chief from 1936 to 1967, whose abstract numerals and lowercase logotype defined the world's model corporate image.

principles.name: Show the idea, not the machine
principles.idea: Evoke what a product does through abstraction rather than depicting it.
principles.example: Olivetti calculating-machine posters of cascading numerals, 1940s-50s

principles.name: The logotype as signature
principles.idea: A lowercase, wide-spaced sans wordmark as the company's voice.

principles.name: Painterly modernism
principles.idea: Colour fields and playful shapes on a structured page.

figures.name: Max Huber
figures.summary: Swiss designer in Milan who bridged Zürich constructivism and Italian colour, with overprinted, kinetic posters and La Rinascente's mark.

principles.name: Transparency and overlap
principles.idea: Colour planes, type and photographs layered as if transparent to create depth and speed.
principles.example: Gran Premio dell'Autodromo di Monza poster, 1948

principles.name: Swiss order, Italian colour
principles.idea: A constructive base carrying saturated, festive colour.

figures.name: Madiha Omar
figures.summary: Iraqi painter, generally seen as the first modern artist to build abstract paintings from Arabic letters (Washington, 1949).

principles.name: The letter as abstract element
principles.idea: Calligraphy as inspiration for abstract form, not as text.
principles.example: Arabic Calligraphy: An Element of Inspiration in Abstract Art, 1949

principles.name: Secular use of a sacred script
principles.idea: Arabic letters in secular modern painting.
principles.example: 48 paintings at the Ibn Sina exhibition, Baghdad, 1952

keyWorks.title: Arabic Calligraphy: An Element of Inspiration in Abstract Art

figures.name: Bruno Munari
figures.summary: Milanese artist-designer of useless machines, unreadable books and programmed art, who treated play and systematic variation as design method.

principles.name: Play as method
principles.idea: Curiosity and play are serious design tools.

principles.name: Variation from one element
principles.idea: Generate many forms by systematically varying one thing.
principles.example: Declinazione grafica del nome Campari poster, 1964

principles.name: Design as ordinary craft
principles.idea: The designer is a craftsman of everyday life, not a genius.

figures.name: Alexey Brodovitch
figures.summary: Harper's Bazaar art director 1934–58 who made the magazine a cinematic sequence of bled photographs and white space, and taught a generation of photographers.

principles.name: Cinematic pacing
principles.idea: A magazine is an edited sequence; spreads rhyme, accelerate and pause like film.

principles.name: Type takes the shape of the picture
principles.idea: Text blocks are cut to echo the forms in the photograph.

principles.name: Shock value on every page
principles.idea: Each page must surprise; never show the reader what they have seen before.

keyWorks.title: Observations (with Richard Avedon and Truman Capote)

figures.name: Ladislav Sutnar
figures.summary: Czech avant-gardist stranded in New York in 1939 who, at Sweet's Catalog Service, invented much of modern information design and navigation.

principles.name: Visual flow
principles.idea: A document is designed as a path, leading the eye from general to specific by size, colour, position and sign.

principles.name: Function, not decoration
principles.idea: Every bar, tab and circled numeral has a navigational job.

principles.name: Punctuation as structure
principles.idea: Brackets, rules and numerals organise information; he is credited with parenthesised area codes.

keyWorks.title: Package Design: The Force of Visual Selling

figures.name: Geraldo de Barros
figures.role: Photographer, painter, graphic and furniture designer
figures.summary: Abstract photographer and Ruptura founder who moved concrete art into industry: Unilabor furniture, the Forminform design office and mass-produced modern objects.

principles.name: Cut the negative
principles.idea: Photographs are constructed by scratching, masking and multiple exposure, so the camera produces form rather than records it.

principles.name: Art for the masses through production
principles.idea: Modern design reaches people through cooperatives and factories, not galleries.

principles.name: The right to error
principles.idea: He treated mistakes as part of the method; error is how new form appears.
principles.example: Sobras, his last photographs, made with Ana Moraes, from 1996

keyWorks.title: IV Centenário de São Paulo festival posters (with Alexandre Wollner)

figures.name: Marcello Nizzoli
figures.summary: Olivetti's chief product designer, whose sculptural Lexikon 80 and Lettera 22 made the office machine a warm, unified object.

principles.name: The product as sculpture
principles.idea: One softly modelled shell unifies the mechanism.

principles.name: Portable and personal
principles.idea: Mechanical precision in a light, friendly object for one person.

principles.name: Integration of the arts
principles.idea: Product, graphic and architectural design as one practice.
principles.example: ENI office building, San Donato Milanese, 1956-58

figures.name: Max Bill
figures.summary: Bauhaus-trained concrete artist who linked Bauhaus pedagogy to Swiss design and co-founded, designed and first led the Ulm school.

principles.name: Concrete form
principles.idea: Build design and art from pure, measurable relationships rather than imitation.

principles.name: Good form
principles.idea: Judge everyday objects on the union of use, material and beauty, and show the good ones publicly.

principles.name: The multifunctional object
principles.idea: One simple form should serve many uses.

figures.name: Saul Bass
figures.summary: Turned film titles into a prologue and posters into one cut-paper symbol, then built some of America's longest-lived corporate marks.

principles.name: Symbolize and summarize
principles.idea: Reduce a whole film or company to one graphic sign used everywhere.
principles.example: The Man with the Golden Arm poster and titles, 1955

principles.name: Titles as prologue
principles.idea: The credit sequence sets mood and theme before the first scene.

principles.name: Making the ordinary extraordinary
principles.idea: Familiar things are shown in an unfamiliar way.
principles.example: Walk on the Wild Side title sequence, 1962

principles.name: Marks that outlive companies
principles.idea: Simple symbolic logos designed to last decades.

keyWorks.title: The Man with the Golden Arm

images.title: The Man with the Golden Arm

figures.name: Kiyoshi Awazu
figures.summary: Self-taught activist designer who designed the Metabolist manifesto and fused folklore, protest and supergraphics.

principles.name: Design sides with the dispossessed
principles.idea: The poster as solidarity with people excluded from power.
principles.example: Umi o Kaese (Give Back Our Oceans), 1955

principles.name: Reproduction as method
principles.idea: Recurring motifs such as fingerprints and turtles reprinted and transformed for decades.
principles.example: A Diversity of Birds, Hiroshima Appeals, 1984

principles.name: Graphics at architectural scale
principles.idea: Supergraphics wrap a whole building.

figures.name: Waldemar Świerzy
figures.summary: Prolific Polish School portraitist, with more than 1,500 posters, who brought gestural painting, pop-art and folk art into the poster.

principles.name: Bring painting into the poster
principles.idea: Gesture, lyrical abstraction and pop-art go straight onto the sheet.
principles.example: Hej kolęda poster for No To Co, 1968

principles.name: The portrait as sign
principles.idea: A few traits plus a metaphor for the profession.

principles.name: Legible only at a distance
principles.idea: Up close a mesh of squiggles and dots; from afar a face.

figures.name: Augusto de Campos
figures.summary: Noigandres poet whose colour-coded Poetamenos (1955) launched Brazilian concrete poetry, and who carried the method into poster-poems, objects and digital media.

principles.name: Colour as voice
principles.idea: Each colour in a poem marks a different voice or timbre, like a score.

principles.name: The poem as poster
principles.idea: Political poems are printed as large-format posters made from found commercial type.

principles.name: The reader assembles it
principles.idea: Pop-up and folding structures make reading physical and interactive.

figures.name: Paul Rand
figures.summary: Gave American design its theory in Thoughts on Design and its corporate face in IBM, Westinghouse, UPS and ABC: the idea first, delivered with play.

principles.name: The idea
principles.idea: Design starts from a concept that reconciles the client's problem with a visual form; without it everything is decoration.

principles.name: Play
principles.idea: Design is a game with rules; wit and surprise make a problem solvable and memorable.
principles.example: Essay Design and the Play Instinct, in Kepes's Education of Vision, 1965

principles.name: Form and content
principles.idea: Content is what is said, form is how; good design fuses them and makes the commonplace strange.

principles.name: Simplicity and restraint
principles.idea: A mark must survive blurring, reduction and misuse.

figures.name: Charles and Ray Eames
figures.role: Designers: furniture, film, exhibition, architecture (the Eames Office)
figures.summary: Husband-and-wife office (Charles 1907–1978, Ray 1912–1988) that made furniture, toys, films and exhibitions one discipline of learning by doing.

principles.name: Learning by doing
principles.idea: Prototype endlessly; the model is the argument.
principles.example: Moulded plywood experiments leading to the LCW chair, 1946

principles.name: The best for the most for the least
principles.idea: Industrial production serves good design for ordinary people.

principles.name: Powers of scale
principles.idea: Understand a system by seeing it at every scale.

principles.name: Design depends on constraints
principles.idea: Recognise as many constraints as possible and work within them with enthusiasm.

keyWorks.title: Mathematica: A World of Numbers... and Beyond

images.title: Eames Lounge Chair and Ottoman
images.credit: The original uploader was Sonett72 at English Wikipedia.

figures.name: Louis Danziger
figures.summary: Los Angeles modernist, taught by Lustig and Brodovitch, who brought Constructivist structure to American advertising and then taught design history for decades.

principles.name: Constructivist form for ordinary products
principles.idea: Diagonals, photography and type as structure, applied to everyday advertising.

principles.name: Clarity as intelligence
principles.idea: Respect the reader enough to say one thing.
principles.example: Container Corporation of America print ad, 1958

principles.name: Teach the history
principles.idea: A designer's longest-lasting work can be teaching where solutions came from.

keyWorks.title: New York School exhibition poster, LACMA

figures.name: Hans Gugelot
figures.summary: Ulm's head of product design, who gave Braun its new product language and made the module the basis of furniture and appliances.

principles.name: Modular systems
principles.idea: Products built from a standard module so they can grow and combine.
principles.example: M125 storage system for Bofinger, 125 mm module, from 1950

principles.name: The product as a quiet box
principles.idea: Strip furniture pretensions and expose function in a clean volume.

principles.name: Ergonomics as form-giver
principles.idea: Use and production determine shape.
principles.example: Kodak Carousel-S slide projector with Reinhold Häcker, 1963

figures.name: Dieter Rams
figures.summary: Braun's head of design (1961-97) and Vitsœ's designer, whose 'less, but better' and ten principles define functionalist product design.

principles.name: Useful, understandable, honest
principles.idea: Good design is innovative, makes a product useful, aesthetic and understandable, and never overstates what it is.

principles.name: Unobtrusive and long-lasting
principles.idea: Products are neutral tools that avoid fashion and last; good design is environmentally friendly.

principles.name: Thorough to the last detail
principles.idea: Nothing arbitrary or left to chance; care shows respect for the user.

principles.name: As little design as possible
principles.idea: Less, but better: concentrate on essentials, back to purity and simplicity.

images.title: Braun TS 45, TG 60 and L 450 hi-fi

figures.name: Décio Pignatari
figures.summary: Noigandres poet whose 'beba coca cola' turned a slogan into an anti-advertisement, and who taught information theory and semiotics to Brazilian designers.

principles.name: Detourn the slogan
principles.idea: The grammar of advertising, short words and repetition, is rearranged until it critiques itself.

principles.name: Information before ornament
principles.idea: Communication theory, how much a sign carries, is a design tool.

keyWorks.title: Teoria da Poesia Concreta (with the Campos brothers)

figures.name: Gerd Leufert
figures.summary: German-trained émigré who made El Farol and the Museo de Bellas Artes into laboratories, and staged Venezuela's first graphic design exhibition in 1961.

principles.name: The client publication as experiment
principles.idea: An oil company's magazine is used to test a new graphic language, free of folkloric illustration.

principles.name: The museum as client and stage
principles.idea: Museum catalogues and exhibitions both practise and present design.
principles.example: Gráfica 1, Museo de Bellas Artes, Caracas, 1961

keyWorks.title: Venezuelan pavilion emblem, New York World's Fair

figures.name: Adrian Frutiger
figures.summary: Type designer across metal, film and digital whose Univers made the type family a numbered system and whose Frutiger set the standard for signage.

principles.name: The family as a system
principles.idea: Design all weights and widths at once, named by a numbering grid instead of adjectives.

principles.name: Legibility in motion
principles.idea: Wayfinding letters must stay open and distinct at distance, angle and speed.
principles.example: Frutiger, from the Charles de Gaulle Airport signage, 1976

principles.name: Design for the machine
principles.idea: Work with the reproduction technology's constraints while staying humane.

figures.name: Max Miedinger
figures.summary: Zürich typesetter who drew Neue Haas Grotesk for Eduard Hoffmann in 1957, renamed Helvetica in 1960.

principles.name: Refine, don't invent
principles.idea: Start from trusted models and remove their quirks.
principles.example: Neue Haas Grotesk, refined from Akzidenz-Grotesk and Schelter-Grotesk references, 1957

principles.name: Uniformity as voice
principles.idea: Tight spacing, horizontal terminals and a large x-height make a dense, even, impersonal texture.

figures.name: Will Burtin
figures.summary: German émigré who art-directed Fortune and then gave science a human scale, most famously in the walk-in model The Cell.

principles.name: Make the invisible visible
principles.idea: Scientific processes are given physical form at human scale.

principles.name: Teach under pressure
principles.idea: Instruction must work for a frightened novice in a moving aircraft.

principles.name: Integration
principles.idea: Art, science and technology are one design problem.

figures.name: Haroldo de Campos
figures.summary: Noigandres co-founder and theorist whose idea of translation as creative re-making ('transcreation') gave concrete poetry its intellectual reach.

principles.name: Transcreation
principles.idea: Translation re-creates form as well as meaning, so the visual and sonic structure of a text is what gets carried over.
principles.example: His translations collected alongside the concrete theory of Teoria da Poesia Concreta, 1965

principles.name: Structure over line
principles.idea: The poem's spatial structure, not the verse line, is the unit of composition.

keyWorks.title: Teoria da Poesia Concreta (with Augusto de Campos and Décio Pignatari)

figures.name: Alexandre Wollner
figures.summary: Ulm-trained 'father of Brazilian modern design', co-founder of Forminform and ESDI, whose constructed marks defined Brazilian corporate identity.

principles.name: Construct the mark
principles.idea: Symbols are built from simple geometric parts (semicircles, triangles, lozenges) so they can be redrawn, scaled and remembered.
principles.example: Sardinhas Coqueiro mark and packaging, Forminform, 1958

principles.name: Research before form
principles.idea: Identity starts from historical and functional research, so form and colour are argued from the client's history rather than chosen for mood.
principles.example: Banco Itaú mark, adopted 1973, later recoloured orange by DPZ's Francesc Petit, a change criticised for ignoring the original research

principles.name: Concrete art as a design grammar
principles.idea: The concrete painter's training in proportion and the module carries straight into identity work.

keyWorks.title: Cinemateca Brasileira logotype (for the MAM Filmoteca)

figures.name: Henryk Tomaszewski
figures.summary: Father of the Polish Poster School; five Vienna first prizes in 1948 and head of the Warsaw Academy poster studio, 1952–1985.

principles.name: Strip to the sign
principles.idea: Analyse, discard the superfluous, drop the adjectives, arrive at a shortcut sign.

principles.name: The lettering is the image
principles.idea: His own handwriting increasingly becomes the whole poster.

principles.name: Train the eye, not the hand
principles.idea: Teach through abstract concepts set as riddles to be solved.

figures.name: Nedo Mion Ferrario
figures.summary: Milan-born Caracas designer, known as Nedo, who art-directed El Farol for thirteen years and drew around sixty geometric, 'impossible' and reversible alphabets.

principles.name: The total magazine
principles.idea: Paper changes, flaps, cover-to-body flow and halftone experiments make the turning of the page itself the design.

principles.name: Impossible letters
principles.idea: Alphabets built on optical paradox (impossible, reversible, computable) are still legible type.
principles.example: Reversibles exhibition, Museo de Bellas Artes, 1969

principles.name: Teach for decades
principles.idea: A design chair held for 27 years forms a national profession.
principles.example: Design chair at the Escuela de Artes Plásticas Cristóbal Rojas, from 1959

figures.name: Siegfried Odermatt
figures.summary: Self-taught Zürich designer who kept the Swiss grid but added wit, overlap and surprise, in partnership with Rosmarie Tissi from 1968.

principles.name: Constructive form with a twist
principles.idea: Keep grid and sans-serif, then break the expected order to make an image.

principles.name: Type as image
principles.idea: Letters overlap, tilt and scale until the word is the illustration.

figures.name: Choi Jeong-ho
figures.summary: Drew the myeongjo and gothic Hangul types of the 1950s-60s on which nearly every later Korean text face is based.

principles.name: The text face as infrastructure
principles.idea: Two families, myeongjo and gothic, designed for reading at national scale.

principles.name: Balance inside the square
principles.idea: Each syllable block drawn so its optical colour matches its neighbours across thousands of combinations.

figures.name: Josef Müller-Brockmann
figures.summary: The Zürich master of the grid: Tonhalle concert posters, Der Film, Neue Grafik and the book that codified the modular grid.

principles.name: The grid as attitude
principles.idea: The grid is a way of thinking: the will to order, clarify and reach the essential.

principles.name: Music made visible
principles.idea: Geometric rhythms express music's structure without illustrating it.
principles.example: Tonhalle Musica Viva concert posters, from 1950

principles.name: Clarity as civic duty
principles.idea: Public posters are a public service, so clarity is an ethical demand.

figures.name: Yusaku Kamekura
figures.summary: 'The Boss' of postwar Japanese design: Tokyo 1964 emblem and posters, Nikon, NTT, co-founder of NDC and first JAGDA president.

principles.name: Geometry plus light
principles.idea: Pure geometric forms made to glow through colour gradation and photography.

principles.name: Photograph the decisive instant
principles.idea: Build the poster on one technically demanding photograph.

principles.name: The mark as monument
principles.idea: Identities meant to outlast their companies' strategies.

keyWorks.title: Trademarks and Symbols of the World

figures.name: Franciszek Starowieyski
figures.summary: Baroque-surrealist of the Polish School: skulls, anatomy and mock-17th-century calligraphy turned the poster into an autonomous artwork.

principles.name: The baroque as resistance
principles.idea: Morbid, ornamental imagery against both Socialist Realism and cheerful circus posters.

principles.name: The poster as autonomous work
principles.idea: Posters as 'Franciszek Starowieyski presents', not as advertisements.

principles.name: Persona as method
principles.idea: From 1970 he back-dated his works by 300 years.

keyWorks.title: Płaczący gołąbek pokoju (The Crying Dove of Peace)

figures.name: Josef Albers
figures.summary: Taught the Bauhaus preliminary course, then Black Mountain and Yale; Interaction of Color made colour an experimental discipline.

principles.name: Colour is relative
principles.idea: A colour changes with its neighbours, so learn by experiment rather than rule.

principles.name: Economy of material
principles.idea: Get the most form from the least material and waste.

principles.name: Modular letters
principles.idea: Build an alphabet from a few geometric parts.

images.title: Studies for Homage to the Square
Armchair
images.credit: Tim Evanson from Cleveland Heights, Ohio, USA

figures.name: Roman Cieślewicz
figures.summary: Polish School photomontagist who moved to Paris in 1963, art-directed Elle and made the halftone dot and mirror image expressive.

principles.name: Maximum picture, maximum information
principles.idea: The poster is the street picture and must hit as hard as possible.

principles.name: Mechanise the image
principles.idea: Enlarged halftone, mirroring and repetition make the image pulse.

principles.name: Montage from the archive
principles.idea: Old masters and press photographs collide into new meaning.

figures.name: Zdeněk Ziegler
figures.summary: Architect-trained typographer of the Czechoslovak New Wave film poster, later book designer, stamp designer and rector of VŠUP Prague.

principles.name: Type chosen for the text's nature
principles.idea: Every typeface decision follows the character of the text.
principles.example: Book series for Odeon and Československý spisovatel, from 1963

principles.name: One designer, one whole
principles.idea: Poster, book series, identity and stamp form one designed world.

figures.name: Juan Carlos Distéfano
figures.summary: Organised the Instituto Di Tella's graphic design department in the 1960s, Argentina's first professional design studio, then became a major figurative sculptor.

principles.name: A horizontal studio
principles.idea: He described the Di Tella team as having no rigid line between those who direct and those who execute.
principles.example: Departamento de Diseño Gráfico, Instituto Di Tella, 1963-1970

principles.name: Swiss structure, New York wit
principles.idea: Swiss order is combined with the idea-led advertising of the New York School inside one institutional voice.
principles.example: Di Tella exhibition posters and catalogues, 1960s

principles.name: Make it by hand, fast and cheap
principles.idea: Small budgets and short deadlines are worked with directly, not hidden.

keyWorks.title: Prize-winning poster for the Siam Di Tella fiftieth anniversary competition

figures.name: Chermayeff & Geismar
figures.role: Identity design firm (Chermayeff & Geismar & Haviv since 2013)
figures.summary: Ivan Chermayeff and Tom Geismar's firm, founded with Robert Brownjohn, which made the abstract corporate symbol American: Chase, Mobil, NBC, PBS.

principles.name: Memorable, appropriate, simple
principles.idea: A mark must be all three; abstraction is allowed when the company cannot be pictured.

principles.name: Type as the mark
principles.idea: A wordmark with one distinctive gesture.

principles.name: Refresh, don't replace
principles.idea: Evolve heritage marks rather than discard their equity.
principles.example: NBC peacock reduced to six feathers, 1986
