images.title: Xerox wordmark
images.credit: The original uploader was Tvwade at English Wikipedia.

figures.name: Ivan Chermayeff
figures.summary: Co-founder of Chermayeff & Geismar whose identity rigour sat alongside hundreds of loose, witty collage posters and children's books.

principles.name: Collage as found wit
principles.idea: Scraps of everyday material assembled into a portrait or scene.
principles.example: Collage posters for Mobil-sponsored public television arts programming, 1970s–80s

principles.name: Words that move
principles.idea: Typography should act out its meaning.
principles.example: Watching Words Move, with Brownjohn and Geismar, 1959

principles.name: Teach shapes first
principles.idea: Basic forms are the first vocabulary of seeing.

images.title: Mobil logo
images.credit: The original uploader was Cheeselouise at English Wikipedia.

figures.name: Lella Vignelli
figures.role: Architect, interior and product designer, studio CEO
figures.summary: Architect and long-under-credited co-founder of Unimark and Vignelli Associates, who led its three-dimensional work and ran the practice.

principles.name: Design is one, in three dimensions
principles.idea: The same discipline governs a plate, a chair and a showroom.

principles.name: Sprezzatura
principles.idea: Rigour that looks effortless.

principles.name: The office as a design
principles.idea: Running the practice, its clients, money and people, is part of the work.

figures.name: Jan Lenica
figures.summary: Poster artist and cut-out animator whose sinuous, multiplied contour revived Art Nouveau line for the 1960s.

principles.name: The contour as a living thing
principles.idea: Flowing multiple outlines carry the image's energy.

principles.name: Poster and animation as one art
principles.idea: Cut-out figures move between street and screen.

principles.name: Absurdity as commentary
principles.idea: Bureaucracy and the machine swallow the individual.

figures.name: Rogério Duarte
figures.summary: Tropicália's graphic designer: Cinema Novo posters and the 1968 Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil covers, mixing Ulm-taught structure with psychedelic colour.

principles.name: Colour researched, then released
principles.idea: Colour is a researched instrument; he described the Deus e o Diabo poster as a new conception of colour born of deep research.
principles.example: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol poster, 1964

principles.name: Know the rules to break them
principles.idea: Grounding in Ulm-style rational design is what lets the pop and psychedelic break land.

principles.name: Design for the left without its clichés
principles.idea: Political graphics need not look like socialist realism; vernacular and pop sources can carry politics.
principles.example: Head of visual arts at the Centro Popular de Cultura (UNE), early 1960s

keyWorks.title: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol poster

images.title: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol

figures.name: Ken Garland
figures.summary: British designer and writer whose 1964 First Things First manifesto asked designers to put their skills to useful work; its 1999 reissue reopened the debate.

principles.name: First things first
principles.idea: Design skill belongs first to useful communication (signs, books, education, science), not to the 'high pitched scream' of consumer selling.

principles.name: Clear form for a cause
principles.idea: Plain, bold modernist graphics serve campaigns and education as well as clients.
principles.example: CND Aldermaston to London Easter march poster, 1962

principles.name: Work is a team effort
principles.idea: He insisted his studio's work was collective, and later argued for partnership with clients over 'us and them'.

figures.name: Karl Gerstner
figures.summary: Basel designer and GGK co-founder who reframed design as writing programmes that generate solutions, the root of parametric and systems design.

principles.name: Programmes for solutions
principles.idea: Design the rules that generate all valid answers rather than one answer.

principles.name: Integral typography
principles.idea: Form and content are one: the word's form expresses its meaning.
principles.example: Typography for Markus Kutter's Schiff nach Europa, 1957

principles.name: Type families as systems
principles.idea: A family can be designed as a mathematical matrix of variants.

figures.name: Bob Noorda
figures.summary: Dutch designer in Milan whose 1964 Metropolitana signage invented modern transit wayfinding, before co-founding Unimark International.

principles.name: Signage as continuous system
principles.idea: Information on a continuous band at fixed height so passengers always know where to look.

principles.name: Consistency at scale
principles.idea: One sans, one colour code, applied everywhere.
principles.example: New York subway wayfinding with Massimo Vignelli at Unimark, late 1960s

images.title: Lombardy regional emblem
images.credit: Pino Tovaglia, Bob Noorda, Roberto Sambonet and Bruno Munari

figures.name: Herb Lubalin
figures.summary: Master of 'typographics' who used phototype to make words into images, from Mother & Child to Avant Garde, ITC and U&lc.

principles.name: Typographics
principles.idea: Type is not set but designed into an image of its own meaning.

principles.name: The logotype as editorial
principles.idea: A masthead can be a manifesto for the magazine it heads.

principles.name: Promote type by showing it off
principles.idea: A type catalogue disguised as a lively magazine sells faces by using them.

keyWorks.title: ITC Avant Garde Gothic (with Tom Carnase)

figures.name: Tadanori Yokoo
figures.summary: Collaged the Rising Sun, kitsch and his own biography into psychedelic posters that broke Japanese modernism's consensus.

principles.name: The self as subject
principles.idea: The designer's own biography is the poster's content.

principles.name: Kitsch and sacred side by side
principles.idea: Pin-ups, Buddhist imagery and national symbols in one plane, at equal weight.
principles.example: A la Maison de M. Civecawa, 1966

principles.name: Restless restyling
principles.idea: Refuse a fixed style; deliberately hang incompatible work together.

keyWorks.title: A la Maison de M. Civecawa

figures.name: Parviz Tanavoli
figures.summary: Key Saqqakhaneh artist whose Heech sculptures cast the Persian word 'nothing' as a solid character.

principles.name: A word as an object
principles.idea: Three nasta'liq letters cast as a figure that sits, is caged or embraced.

principles.name: The craftsman's archive
principles.idea: Locks, rugs and salt bags studied as design sources.

principles.name: Nothingness as content
principles.idea: Sufi creation from nothing, made tangible.

figures.name: Armin Hofmann
figures.summary: Basel teacher whose elementary form exercises and Yale professorship carried the Swiss method into design education worldwide.

principles.name: Elementary form exercises
principles.idea: Teach through systematic exploration of dot, line, plane and letter before any real brief.

principles.name: Contrast as engine
principles.idea: Meaning comes from opposition: large/small, sharp/soft, static/dynamic.

principles.name: Reduction to the sign
principles.idea: A poster should collapse to one memorable form.

keyWorks.title: Graphic Design Manual: Principles and Practice

images.title: Alte und neue Formen in Japan, Gewerbemuseum Basel

figures.name: Kazumasa Nagai
figures.summary: NDC founder member and president, JAGDA's second president, who moved from engraved geometric abstraction to hand-drawn animals.

principles.name: Abstraction as cosmology
principles.idea: Fine engraved line fields that suggest energy and space rather than objects.

principles.name: From abstraction to living creatures
principles.idea: Late work turns to staring animals drawn in ornamental line as a plea for life.

principles.name: The quiet corporate mark
principles.idea: Restrained marks for large institutions.

figures.name: Józef Mroszczak
figures.summary: Co-founder of Projekt magazine and founder of the Warsaw International Poster Biennale, who professionalised Polish design education.

principles.name: Build the institution
principles.idea: A magazine, a biennale and a museum gave the school its international stage.

principles.name: Balance design and expression
principles.idea: Rigorous composition kept painterly.

principles.name: The poster as public conscience
principles.idea: Posters as moral statements, not only announcements.
principles.example: Auschwitz – Never Again project, prize at the 1966 Biennale

figures.name: Aloísio Magalhães
figures.summary: Recife-born designer of Brazil's banknotes, the first Globo symbol and the Rio IV Centenário mark, who co-founded ESDI and later ran national heritage policy.

principles.name: Design for a nation's identity
principles.idea: Currency, anniversaries and broadcasters are where a country meets its own image daily.

principles.name: Pattern as security and beauty
principles.idea: Moiré and mirrored designs make a note both hard to forge and readable whichever way it is held.

principles.name: Heritage is design's raw material
principles.idea: Vernacular craft and cultural memory are the resources a modern design culture builds from.
principles.example: Centro Nacional de Referência Cultural, from 1975

keyWorks.title: IV Centenário do Rio de Janeiro symbol

images.title: First Rede Globo symbol
images.credit: Aloísio Magalhães (original logo). Gabriel dos Santos and Radamistavo (SVG versi

figures.name: Wes Wilson
figures.summary: The Fillmore's poster artist, who adapted Secession lettering into the melting 'psychedelic' letterform that defined the San Francisco poster.

principles.name: Fill the shape
principles.idea: Letters stretch and swell until they fill a silhouette entirely, so the word becomes a shape before it becomes a word.
principles.example: Bill Graham Presents poster 'Fly 8 Miles High with Me', 1966

principles.name: Stop the passer-by
principles.idea: Lettering is built to be 'something people had to stop to figure out', making slowness the hook.
principles.example: Family Dog poster 'The Quick and the Dead', 1966

principles.name: Learn from Vienna
principles.idea: He took the block lettering of the Secession, notably Alfred Roller, and resculpted it rather than inventing from nothing.

keyWorks.title: Fly 8 Miles High with Me (Bill Graham Presents)

figures.name: Seymour Chwast
figures.summary: Push Pin co-founder whose thick, comic line, woodcut sources and display faces made protest and commerce funny.

principles.name: Protest through humour
principles.idea: The anti-war poster as a cartoon can carry more weight than a photograph.

principles.name: The vernacular as source
principles.idea: Woodcut, comics and naive drawing are legitimate design languages.

principles.name: Type that draws
principles.idea: Display faces are illustrations in alphabet form.

images.title: Kiss Kiss Bang Bang
images.credit: Jacket design by Seymour Chwast. Published by Atlantic–Little, Brown Books, an i

figures.name: Eduardo Muñoz Bachs
figures.summary: Self-taught Valencia-born designer of ICAIC's first poster in 1960 and over 2,000 film posters, with a childlike drawn figure and hand lettering.

principles.name: Draw like a child, think like an adult
principles.idea: A naive, comic drawing style and hand-made lettering carry sophisticated irony.

principles.name: The figure is the poster
principles.idea: The human face or whole body dominates; colours are bright but never shocking.
principles.example: En busca de un hombre poster, ICAIC, 1967

principles.name: Volume as a style
principles.idea: Thousands of posters over a lifetime make a recognisable personal language within an institution.
principles.example: No hay regreso para Johnny poster, ICAIC, 1971

figures.name: Alfredo Rostgaard
figures.summary: Guantánamo-born caricaturist who became OSPAAAL's art director in 1966, mixing pop, psychedelia and humour into the most travelled solidarity posters.

principles.name: Humour for serious subjects
principles.idea: Caricature and playfulness make grave political subjects memorable rather than solemn.

principles.name: Borrow the enemy's pop
principles.idea: Warhol-like commercial graphics and psychedelic line are turned to anti-imperialist ends.

principles.name: Silkscreen colour as structure
principles.idea: Flat overprinted inks carry the composition, not just fill it.

figures.name: Victor Moscoso
figures.summary: The one Yale-trained artist among the San Francisco poster makers, who turned Albers's colour theory into posters that vibrate.

principles.name: Colour as motion
principles.idea: Albers's lesson that adjacent colours change each other is applied at full saturation so the poster appears to flicker.

principles.name: Invert the academy
principles.idea: Trained at Cooper Union and Yale, he used that training against itself: academic colour and lettering skill applied to make posters harder to read, not easier.

principles.name: Sequence and loop
principles.idea: His comics repeat frames on a fixed grid so a story can be entered at any panel and read as a cycle.

keyWorks.title: Neon Rose series for the Matrix

figures.name: Emil Ruder
figures.summary: Basel typography teacher who argued modernism to the printing trade and wrote Typographie, the period's defining manual of rhythm and white space.

principles.name: Communication first
principles.idea: Legibility and order come before expression; form is earned by function.

principles.name: Counter-form is form
principles.idea: The white of the page and between letters is designed as deliberately as the black.

principles.name: Rhythm of the word
principles.idea: A line of type has musical rhythm built from letter shapes and intervals.

figures.name: Wim Crouwel
figures.role: Graphic designer, type designer, educator, museum director
figures.summary: 'Mr Gridnik': Total Design co-founder and Stedelijk Museum designer whose visible grids and New Alphabet anticipated screen typography.

principles.name: The grid as visible structure
principles.idea: The grid generates letterforms and images and is shown, not hidden.

principles.name: Accept the machine's limits
principles.idea: Design for what the display technology can render.

principles.name: Neutral, not anonymous
principles.idea: Systematic design can carry a strong signature through custom lettering.

figures.name: Total Design
figures.summary: Amsterdam studio founded by Crouwel, Wissing, Kramer and the Schwarz brothers that brought systematic total identity to Dutch public life.

principles.name: Multidisciplinary by design
principles.idea: Graphics, products, interiors and environments under one roof so identity extends into space.

principles.name: Wayfinding as identity
principles.idea: For a public institution, the signage is the identity.

principles.name: Systematic corporate identity
principles.idea: Logos specified in manuals and applied consistently.

figures.name: George Lois
figures.summary: Creative Revolution provocateur whose Esquire covers made a single staged image into an editorial argument.

principles.name: The Big Idea
principles.idea: One provocative, instantly graspable concept beats a hundred well-made layouts.
principles.example: Muhammad Ali as Saint Sebastian, Esquire, April 1968

principles.name: Image as editorial
principles.idea: A cover is an argument, not a decoration.
principles.example: Andy Warhol in a Campbell's soup can, Esquire, May 1969

principles.name: Speak in the audience's voice
principles.idea: Put the slogan in the mouth of the viewer.

figures.name: Farshid Mesghali
figures.summary: Kanoon illustrator, animator and poster designer; the only Iranian Hans Christian Andersen Award winner (1974).

principles.name: Cross every medium
principles.idea: The same designer makes the book, the film and the poster.
principles.example: The Little Black Fish, 1968; Look Again, 1974

principles.name: Technique follows the story
principles.idea: Lithography, collage, watercolour or lithographed-book style as each story needs.

principles.name: One clear image for an auteur's film
principles.idea: The poster distils the film into a single image.

keyWorks.title: Mahi-ye siyah-e kuchulu (The Little Black Fish)

images.title: Mahi-ye siyah-e kuchulu (The Little Black Fish)
images.credit: Author: Samad Behrangi / Illustrator: Farshid Mesghali

figures.name: Raúl Martínez
figures.summary: Former Los Once abstractionist who became Cuba's pop portraitist of Martí and Camilo Cienfuegos and a designer for ICAIC, Casa de las Américas and OSPAAAL.

principles.name: The hero, multiplied
principles.idea: Portraits of national heroes are repeated in grids of flat colour, pop serialisation turned into revolutionary iconography.
principles.example: Pop portraits of José Martí, mid-1960s

principles.name: Painter and designer as one practice
principles.idea: The same artist moves between painting, book design and posters without a hierarchy.
principles.example: Day of World Solidarity with the Cuban Revolution poster, OSPAAAL, 1968

keyWorks.title: Day of World Solidarity with the Cuban Revolution, 26 July
Lucía film poster (for Humberto Solás's 1968 film)

figures.name: Félix Beltrán
figures.summary: New York-trained Cuban designer who led the government's Comisión de Orientación Revolucionaria posters, taught design from 1963 and moved to Mexico in 1982.

principles.name: Simplicity as effectiveness
principles.idea: One idea, minimum elements: simplicity is the basis of communication that works.

principles.name: Theory alongside practice
principles.idea: A designer writes and publishes on design to build the discipline.
principles.example: Desde el diseño, Havana, 1970; Letragrafía, 1973; Acerca del diseño, 1975

principles.name: The archive as infrastructure
principles.idea: Collecting design builds the discipline's memory.
principles.example: First international graphic design archive in Latin America, Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana, Mexico City

figures.name: Lance Wyman
figures.summary: New Jersey designer who developed the MEXICO68 logotype and its applications, then the Mexico City Metro pictograms and the Washington Metro map.

principles.name: A logo should become a programme
principles.idea: A mark that adapts to signs and environments can drive an entire design programme.
principles.example: Chrysler pavilion pointing-hand logo and signs, New York World's Fair, 1964

principles.name: Functional aesthetic
principles.idea: He credits the no-nonsense functional aesthetic of the sea and the factories he grew up around as a key influence.

principles.name: Clarity over geography
principles.idea: A transit map shows routes, transfers and landmarks clearly rather than distances to scale.
principles.example: Washington Metro map, mid-1970s, revised by Wyman in 2012

images.title: Mexico City Metro station sign, Zapata

figures.name: Eduardo Terrazas
figures.summary: Architect who coordinated the Mexico 68 identity programme and its urban design under Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, then became a painter of systematic geometric series.

principles.name: Identity at city scale
principles.idea: An event's identity is applied to streets, kiosks and pavements so the whole city becomes the medium.

principles.name: Assemble an international team
principles.idea: Local direction plus recruited international designers produce a system neither would alone.
principles.example: Recruiting Lance Wyman and others to the Olympic identity programme, 1966-1968

keyWorks.title: Mexico pavilion, New York World's Fair (with Pedro Ramírez Vázquez)
Mexico 68 identity and urban design programme

figures.name: Douglas Engelbart
figures.summary: Led SRI's Augmentation Research Center and gave the 1968 demo that introduced the mouse, windows, hypertext and real-time collaboration.

principles.name: Augment, don't automate
principles.idea: Computers should amplify human intellect and collective problem-solving, not replace people.
principles.example: Augmenting Human Intellect: A Conceptual Framework, 1962

principles.name: Co-evolve tools and people
principles.idea: Skills, methods and tools must develop together; a tool that demands learning is acceptable if it raises the ceiling.
principles.example: NLS chord keyset plus mouse, demonstrated 1968

principles.name: Bootstrapping
principles.idea: Use the system to build the system, so improvements compound.
principles.example: ARC team developing NLS inside NLS, late 1960s

keyWorks.title: Augmenting Human Intellect: A Conceptual Framework
NLS demonstration ('The Mother of All Demos')

figures.name: Ghobad Shiva
figures.summary: Founder of the graphics departments at Iranian national broadcasting and Soroush, co-founder of IGDS and planner of the first Tehran poster biennial.

principles.name: Iranian themes in a graphic idiom
principles.idea: Persian motifs restated as flat poster shapes.

principles.name: Design departments as infrastructure
principles.idea: In-house studios at broadcasters and publishers as public design.
principles.example: Graphics department of Iranian radio and television, 1968

figures.name: René Azcuy
figures.summary: ICAIC's most austere film-poster designer: black, white and one colour, a single cropped photographic image, and a metaphor instead of a scene.

principles.name: One image, one idea
principles.idea: A single high-contrast photographic fragment stands in for the whole film.

principles.name: Restraint as intensity
principles.idea: Minimal palette and large empty space make violence or desire more charged than illustration would.

figures.name: Peter Max
figures.summary: The New York illustrator who turned the 'Cosmic '60s' look into mass-licensed merchandise, posters and a Life magazine cover.

principles.name: The full spectrum
principles.idea: Rainbow gradients and Day-Glo colour, often the whole visible spectrum in one image, carry optimism directly.

principles.name: Style as licence
principles.idea: A single recognisable manner is applied across posters, clocks, clothing and stamps, making the artist a brand.

figures.name: Unimark International
figures.role: International design firm (Chicago, New York, Milan)
figures.summary: Design firm run like a corporation, briefly the world's largest, that sold grids, Helvetica and manuals instead of artistic personality.

principles.name: Design as a business discipline
principles.idea: Replace the designer-as-artist with standardised, repeatable method.
principles.example: Unimark's corporate structure and client manuals, from 1965

principles.name: Helvetica and the grid as defaults
principles.idea: A neutral typeface on a modular grid lets many hands stay consistent.

principles.name: Identity across every touchpoint
principles.idea: One system governs aircraft, tickets, signs and stationery.

keyWorks.title: New York City Transit Authority Graphics Standards Manual

figures.name: Tomás Maldonado
figures.summary: Buenos Aires concrete painter who co-founded Arte Concreto-Invención, edited Nueva Visión, then shaped the Ulm model as teacher and rector.

principles.name: Design as science-informed method
principles.idea: Design should balance science and making, using planning methods, perception theory and semiotics rather than artistic intuition.

principles.name: Systems over objects
principles.idea: Codes and systems for a company matter more than any single beautiful artefact.
principles.example: Sign and code systems for Olivetti and La Rinascente with Gui Bonsiepe, 1964-1967

principles.name: Design as environmental responsibility
principles.idea: Design has to answer to ecology and society, not only to industry.
principles.example: La speranza progettuale, 1970 (English: Design, Nature, and Revolution, 1972)

figures.name: Guillermo González Ruiz
figures.summary: Architect-designer who led the 1971-72 Buenos Aires signage plan with Ronald Shakespear and directed graphic design at the University of Buenos Aires.

principles.name: Signage is architecture
principles.idea: Wayfinding is designed with an architect's sense of space, sightlines and urban scale.
principles.example: Plan Visual de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, 1971-1972

principles.name: Teach the profession into existence
principles.idea: A public university programme is the way to make design a recognised discipline in a country.
principles.example: Director of Graphic Design at FADU, Universidad de Buenos Aires, 1985-1990

keyWorks.title: Plan Visual de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires (with Ronald Shakespear)

figures.name: Ronald Shakespear
figures.role: Graphic designer, wayfinding and identity designer
figures.summary: Rosario-born designer of Buenos Aires's urban signage, hospital system and Subte wayfinding, and more than a thousand identities.

principles.name: The city as a client
principles.idea: Wayfinding at city scale, for streets, hospitals and subway, is the most public form of graphic design.
principles.example: Municipal hospitals signage, with Raúl Shakespear, 1978

principles.name: A family studio across generations
principles.idea: A practice carries a consistent system language across decades by passing projects to the next generation.
principles.example: Subte signage with Lorenzo and Juan Shakespear, 1995-2008

keyWorks.title: Plan Visual de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires (with Guillermo González Ruiz)

figures.name: Massimo Vignelli
figures.summary: Italian rationalist who systematised American public and corporate design; his Canon is semantics, syntactics, pragmatics and a handful of typefaces.

principles.name: Semantics, syntactics, pragmatics
principles.idea: Find the meaning, give it a consistent grammar of grid, type and colour, then make sure it is understood.

principles.name: Discipline and appropriateness
principles.idea: Self-imposed rules applied to every detail; the solution fits the problem, not a style.

principles.name: Ambiguity, used sparingly
principles.idea: A plurality of meanings can enrich a design, but contradiction usually signals loss of control.

principles.name: A limited typeface set
principles.idea: Garamond, Bodoni, Century Expanded and Helvetica, plus a few more, are enough; it is not the type but what you do with it.

keyWorks.title: NYCTA Graphics Standards Manual (with Bob Noorda)

figures.name: Alan Kay
figures.summary: Conceived the Dynabook and led the Smalltalk work at Xerox PARC that produced overlapping windows and the modern desktop.

principles.name: The computer is a medium
principles.idea: A personal computer is a new medium for thought and expression, like print, not a calculator.
principles.example: Alan Kay and Adele Goldberg, Personal Dynamic Media, 1977

principles.name: Doing with images makes symbols
principles.idea: Interfaces should move from action (mouse) to imagery (icons, windows) to symbols (code), following how children learn.
principles.example: Smalltalk environment on the Xerox Alto, 1970s

principles.name: Design for children of all ages
principles.idea: If a child can author on it, the system is truly general; learnability is the test of power.
principles.example: A Personal Computer for Children of All Ages (Dynabook), 1972

keyWorks.title: A Personal Computer for Children of All Ages (Dynabook)

figures.name: Otl Aicher
figures.summary: Ulm co-founder who built complete identity systems for Lufthansa and the 1972 Munich Olympics, whose grid pictograms became the world's signage language.

principles.name: Identity as complete system
principles.idea: One manual governs type, colour, grid, photography and signs everywhere.

principles.name: Pictograms on a grid
principles.idea: Signs built only from orthogonal and 45-degree lines so the family reads as one language.

principles.name: Colour as politics
principles.idea: A deliberately light, un-German palette recasts a nation's image.
principles.example: Munich 1972 palette: blue, green, silver, white, orange, no red or black

figures.name: Wiktor Górka
figures.summary: Polish School film-poster master of the fused emblem, best known for Cabaret, who carried the method to Cuba and Mexico.

principles.name: The composite emblem
principles.idea: Two motifs fuse into a third, damning meaning.
principles.example: Kabaret: dancers' legs and Joel Grey's face form a swastika, 1973

principles.name: Teaching as export
principles.idea: The school's method carried abroad through workshops and teaching.
principles.example: Design workshops in Havana, 1970; teaching in Mexico to the mid-1990s

images.title: Pracujemy w trójkę, budujemy za dwunastu

figures.name: Rosmarie Tissi
figures.summary: Odermatt's partner from 1968, who loosened Swiss constructivism into bright, colliding, playful geometry.

principles.name: Playful geometry
principles.idea: Geometric forms arranged for tension and humour rather than equilibrium.
principles.example: Posters for Englersatz and cultural clients, 1980s

principles.name: Letterforms as display objects
principles.idea: A typeface can be a graphic voice in its own right.

figures.name: Shigeo Fukuda
figures.summary: 'Japan's Escher': anti-war and environmental posters built on a single visual paradox, and illusion sculptures.

principles.name: One twist does all the work
principles.idea: Reduce the argument to a single impossible image.

principles.name: Figure-ground ambiguity
principles.idea: Two readings in one silhouette.

principles.name: Illusion leaves the page
principles.idea: The same logic built in three dimensions.

figures.name: Eiko Ishioka
figures.role: Art director, graphic and costume designer
figures.summary: Parco's art director in the 1970s, then a total designer of film, stage and costume, with an Oscar for Dracula.

principles.name: Advertise an attitude
principles.idea: Sell a stance of independence and eroticism, showing almost no product.

principles.name: Total art direction
principles.idea: Poster, set and costume as one designed world.
principles.example: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters, 1985

principles.name: Uncompromising originality
principles.idea: Refuse borrowed style; every project from first principles.

keyWorks.title: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters (production design)

figures.name: Larry Tesler
figures.summary: At PARC and Apple he championed modeless interaction and, with Tim Mott, cut, copy and paste.

principles.name: No modes
principles.idea: A key or click should always do the same thing; hidden modes are the main source of user error.

principles.name: Conservation of complexity
principles.idea: Every application has irreducible complexity; the question is whether the user or the designer absorbs it.
principles.example: Tesler's Law, articulated at Apple in the 1980s

principles.name: Test with real users
principles.idea: Watch non-programmers use the system and change the design to fit them.
principles.example: Gypsy, built for and tested with editors at Xerox's publishing subsidiary Ginn & Co., 1975

figures.name: Cho Young-jae
figures.summary: Introduced corporate identity to Korea, proposed the first non-square Hangul module, and chaired the Seoul 1988 Olympic design committee.

principles.name: Design as thinking work
principles.idea: The designer as strategist and manager, not decorator.

principles.name: The non-square module
principles.idea: Hangul letters with fixed shapes so machines can set the script beautifully.
principles.example: Paper on Hangul mechanisation, Johyeong no. 1, 1976

figures.name: Mohammad Ehsai
figures.summary: Pioneer of Iranian calligraphic painting (naqqashi-khatt) who enlarged and interlaced letters into monumental abstract structures.

principles.name: Enlarge until meaning yields to rhythm
principles.idea: Letters repeated and interlaced become architecture.

principles.name: Mastery first, then rupture
principles.idea: Full classical training underwrites the modern break.
principles.example: Calligraphy for the Reza Abbasi Museum mark, 1976

figures.name: Milton Glaser
figures.summary: Push Pin co-founder, New York magazine co-founder and author of I♥NY, who argued that style is a means and just enough is more.

principles.name: Just enough is more
principles.idea: Neither modernist reduction nor ornament by reflex, just enough to make the idea live.

principles.name: Style is not to be trusted
principles.idea: Any style can serve an idea; none is a virtue in itself.

principles.name: Design for civic good
principles.idea: A mark can change how people feel about a place.

figures.name: Kohei Sugiura
figures.role: Graphic and book designer, researcher of Asian iconography
figures.summary: Architect-trained designer who made the book, magazine and diagram serious media in Japan and taught a generation of Asian book designers.

principles.name: Self-proliferating design
principles.idea: One generative pattern re-run through rotations and colours produces a whole series from the same plates.

principles.name: The cover is a face
principles.idea: The cover answers the contents of each issue.
principles.example: Covers for SD and Toshi Jutaku, late 1960s

principles.name: The book as architecture
principles.idea: Design starts from vertical Mincho body text and works outward to the binding.

keyWorks.title: Mandala: Now You See It, Now You Don't

figures.name: Jamie Reid
figures.summary: The Sex Pistols' designer, who brought Situationist-style détournement and ransom-note lettering from a radical press into the record shop.

principles.name: Ransom note
principles.idea: Headline letters cut from newspapers and glued at random sizes make every word look stolen and every message anonymous.
principles.example: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols, 1977

principles.name: Deface the official image
principles.idea: A sanctioned portrait is altered just enough to turn it against itself.
principles.example: 'God Save the Queen' sleeve, from a Cecil Beaton photograph, 1977

principles.name: Graphics as agitation
principles.idea: Design comes from a political press, not an agency; the sleeve continues the pamphlet.

keyWorks.title: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols

images.title: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols

figures.name: Wolfgang Weingart
figures.summary: The Basel teacher who took Swiss typography as a starting point and 'blew it apart', and whose students carried New Wave to America.

principles.name: Start from Swiss, then question it
principles.idea: Keep the base of Swiss typography (sans serif, asymmetry, the grid) and test every one of its rules to destruction.

principles.name: Typography as craft experiment
principles.idea: Letterspacing, stepped lines and reversed type are explored by hand in hot metal and film, so experiment stays physical.

principles.name: Teach, don't impose
principles.idea: He insisted he never forced a style on students; the 'Weingart style' was what students picked up and spread.
principles.example: Weiterbildungsklasse, Basel School of Design, from 1968

figures.name: Bradbury Thompson
figures.summary: Turned a paper company's promotion, Westvaco Inspirations, into a laboratory where printing's own process colours and plates became the image.

principles.name: Process as image
principles.idea: Separations, halftone dots and printing plates become the illustration.

principles.name: Old and new together
principles.idea: Antique engravings sit beside modern type and colour.

principles.name: Reform the alphabet
principles.idea: Question the two-case system with one form per letter.

principles.name: Read as spoken
principles.idea: Break lines by phrase and cadence, not by measure.

figures.name: Helmi El Touni
figures.role: Painter, book and magazine designer, illustrator
figures.summary: Egyptian painter-designer of more than 3,000 book covers across Cairo and Beirut, setting popular imagery in a flat modern frame.

principles.name: Popular imagery, modern frame
principles.idea: Folk and popular-print motifs restated in flat poster colour.
principles.example: UNICEF International Year of the Child poster, 1979

principles.name: The cover as a repeated public gallery
principles.idea: Volume makes one hand a shared visual language.

keyWorks.title: International Year of the Child poster (UNICEF)

figures.name: Barney Bubbles
figures.role: Graphic designer, art director, video director
figures.summary: Swiss-trained, mostly uncredited sleeve designer for Hawkwind, Stiff and Elvis Costello, who treated all of design history as a palette.

principles.name: History as a palette
principles.idea: Constructivism, Kandinsky, Pop and 1950s packaging are quoted freely, each chosen to say something about the record.
principles.example: Nick Lowe, Labour of Lust 'Hamer & sickle' logo, 1979

principles.name: Errors on purpose
principles.idea: Miscropping, wrong photographs and erratum stickers are designed in, rewarding the fan who notices.
principles.example: The Damned, Damned Damned Damned sleeve with deliberate wrong photo, 1977

principles.name: The sleeve as a kit
principles.idea: Fold-outs, die-cut postcards and build-it pyramids make the package an object to handle and assemble.

principles.name: Anonymity
principles.idea: From 1973 he mostly left his name off the work or used pseudonyms, so the band and the idea stayed in front.

figures.name: Peter Saville
figures.summary: Factory Records' co-founder and designer, who answered punk's mess with Tschichold, scientific plots and appropriated paintings.

principles.name: The cool answer to punk
principles.idea: He took the restrained New Typography of Tschichold as a parallel to the new wave coming out of punk.

principles.name: Appropriate and recontextualise
principles.idea: An image from another field (a pulsar plot, a Fantin-Latour still life) is lifted whole and made to stand for a record.

principles.name: Withhold the name
principles.idea: Band names and titles are small, coded or absent, so the sleeve reads as an artwork and the fan has to know.
principles.example: New Order, Blue Monday die-cut sleeve, 1983

figures.name: Jef Raskin
figures.summary: Conceived the Macintosh project in 1979 as an inexpensive appliance and later codified humane interface design.

principles.name: The information appliance
principles.idea: A computer should be a single-purpose-feeling appliance, ready to use without configuration.

principles.name: Design for habit
principles.idea: Users form habits; interfaces must be monotonous (one way to do a thing) and modeless so habits never betray them.

figures.name: Kan Tai-keung
figures.summary: Former tailor turned Hong Kong's leading Chinese designer, uniting ink painting with modernist identity, from the Bank of China to Chongqing.

principles.name: Ink as a design element
principles.idea: Literati ink-wash brought into the modernist poster as a pure field of tone.

principles.name: Archaic form, modern geometry
principles.idea: An ancient object redrawn as a modern mark that carries a second reading.

principles.name: The city as a character
principles.idea: A civic identity built from one written character.

figures.name: Ikko Tanaka
figures.summary: Rebuilt Rinpa painting from flat geometry, art-directed the Seibu/Saison group's culture and created Muji's no-brand identity.

principles.name: Rinpa from geometry
principles.idea: Rinpa's flat colour fields reconstructed from circles, squares and bands.

principles.name: Design as cultural programming
principles.idea: The art director as curator of a whole culture of shops, theatres and museums.
principles.example: Seibu Museum of Art art direction, 1975-1986

principles.name: The no-brand brand
principles.idea: Remove the logo and let packaging material carry the identity.

figures.name: Neville Brody
figures.role: Graphic designer, art director, type designer
figures.summary: Art director of The Face, who drew custom geometric headline type and then founded FUSE to make type itself experimental.

principles.name: Draw the headline
principles.idea: Instead of buying display type, he drew constructivist-influenced alphabets for each magazine, so the publication's voice was its letterforms.

principles.name: The page as a poster
principles.idea: Magazine pages are composed like posters, with type rotated, scaled and used as image.

principles.name: Type as experiment
principles.idea: A publication ships new, often unusable fonts with essays, to treat typography as research rather than product.

figures.name: Ettore Sottsass
figures.summary: Olivetti's designer who brought colour and play to office machines, then founded Memphis to attack good taste head on.

principles.name: Bring the office into pop culture
principles.idea: A typewriter is coloured, named and marketed like a toy or a fashion item instead of equipment.
principles.example: Valentine typewriter, with Perry A. King, 1969

principles.name: Refuse the consumerist product
principles.idea: Objects become sculptural statements that question consumption rather than serve it.

principles.name: Radical, funny, outrageous
principles.idea: Design is made to provoke and amuse, against prevailing 'good taste'.

figures.name: Henry Steiner
figures.summary: Paul Rand's student who arrived in Hong Kong in 1961 and defined cross-cultural corporate identity, from HSBC to Hongkong Land.

principles.name: One element from each side
principles.idea: A Western structure paired with one specific Chinese form, never a pastiche.
principles.example: Hongkong Land H mark with the character for longevity

principles.name: Equity over novelty
principles.idea: Refresh an inherited mark rather than replace it.
principles.example: Hong Kong Jockey Club monogram, redrawn before 1997

principles.name: Banknotes as public storytelling
principles.idea: A currency's imagery as a coherent narrative system.
principles.example: Standard Chartered Hong Kong notes with mythical creatures

figures.name: Rudy VanderLans
figures.summary: Dutch-trained founder, editor and designer of Emigre magazine, who made it the main forum for, and against, digital-era graphic design.

principles.name: The magazine as forum
principles.idea: A design magazine publishes argument as well as work, inviting guest editors and critics, including opponents.

principles.name: Specimen as design work
principles.idea: The type specimen is a designed artefact that makes you want the face and then shows how to use it.

principles.name: Change format with purpose
principles.idea: The magazine shrank from tabloid to letter size, to CD booklet, to book, as its content shifted from image to text.

keyWorks.title: Emigre: Graphic Design into the Digital Realm

figures.name: Bill Atkinson
figures.summary: Wrote QuickDraw, MacPaint and HyperCard, inventing the menu bar, marching ants, the lasso and fast round rectangles.

principles.name: Speed is a design property
principles.idea: An interface only feels direct if drawing is instant; performance engineering is interface design.

principles.name: Tools you can see working
principles.idea: Selection and editing are made visible (marching ants, FatBits zoom) so the user always knows the state.

principles.name: Authoring for everyone
principles.idea: Give non-programmers cards, buttons and a simple script so they build their own software.

figures.name: Susan Kare
figures.summary: Drew the original Macintosh icons and bitmap typefaces on graph paper, setting the visual grammar of the personal computer.

principles.name: Icons as road signs
principles.idea: An icon must be read instantly at small size, so reduce to the one silhouette that carries the meaning.
principles.example: Macintosh Trash, Paintbrush and Scissors icons, 1984

principles.name: Meaning in a 32-by-32 grid
principles.idea: Every pixel is a decision; constraint produces clarity and a hand-made warmth.
principles.example: Kare's graph-paper icon notebooks, 1983, acquired by MoMA in 2015

principles.name: Wit makes the machine human
principles.idea: A small joke or face (a smiling computer, a dogcow) makes software feel friendly rather than clerical.

figures.name: Ahn Sang-soo
figures.summary: Founder of Ahn Graphics whose 1985 Ahn typeface freed Hangul from the square; Gutenberg Prize 2007 and founder of PaTI.

principles.name: Unlock the square
principles.idea: Fixed-shape letters and the first variable-width Hangul face.

principles.name: Typography as poetry
principles.idea: Letters as a visual score, informed by Yi Sang's typographic poems.
principles.example: Doctoral study of Yi Sang's poetry, 1995

principles.name: Play as pedagogy
principles.idea: Learning by making, outside the official academy.

keyWorks.title: Korean translation of Emil Ruder's Typographie

figures.name: Morteza Momayez
figures.summary: Father of modern Iranian graphic design: Persian-letter marks, Tehran Film Festival art direction, and founder of the profession's schools and societies.

principles.name: A mark from the letters' own rhythm
principles.idea: Initials in Persian script generate the monogram.
principles.example: Iranian Association of Certified Accountants mark, 1974

principles.name: Derive the symbol from local form
principles.idea: City gates become a flower; Maragheh brickwork becomes a car marque.

principles.name: The designer builds the profession
principles.idea: Atelier, syndicate, biennials, society and magazine.
principles.example: Iranian Graphic Designers Society, founding president, 1997

images.title: Iranian Association of Certified Accountants mark

figures.name: Zuzana Licko
figures.summary: Co-founder of Emigre Fonts, who drew the first Macintosh bitmap faces from the pixel up, then remade Baskerville and Bodoni for the digital page.

principles.name: Start from the constraint
principles.idea: Coarse screens and dot-matrix printers dictate the letter; the font is designed for 72 dots per inch rather than forced from metal.

principles.name: Legibility is habit
principles.idea: 'You read best what you read most': familiarity, not form, makes type readable.

principles.name: Revival as reinterpretation
principles.idea: A historical model is reworked for new uses, with a low x-height and abundant ligatures rather than a faithful copy.

figures.name: April Greiman
figures.summary: Weingart's student who brought Basel New Wave to Los Angeles and was among the first to make the Macintosh a design medium.

principles.name: Objects in space
principles.idea: Type, swatches, lines and photographs float in a layered, illusionistic depth instead of sitting on the flat page.

principles.name: Use the crude tool
principles.idea: Low-resolution video capture and early Mac bitmaps are embraced as expressive material, not apologised for.
principles.example: Design Quarterly 133: Does It Make Sense?, 1986

principles.name: Hybrid imagery
principles.idea: Photography, video and type are fused into a single image so the medium boundaries disappear.

keyWorks.title: Design Quarterly 133: Does It Make Sense?

Graphic Design in America, Walker Art Center

figures.name: Rubén Fontana
figures.summary: Di Tella designer who ran its department in 1969-70, then built Argentine typographic culture through tipoGráfica magazine and the Fontana ND typeface.

principles.name: Typography is culture, not styling
principles.idea: A magazine and a school can make typography a shared intellectual discipline for a region.

principles.name: A Latin American text face
principles.idea: Text typefaces can be designed from the region for international distribution.
principles.example: Fontana ND, published by Neufville Digital

keyWorks.title: Co-direction of the Di Tella graphic design department

figures.name: Ed Fella
figures.summary: A Detroit commercial artist for thirty years who made exuberantly 'wrong' hand-built typography for gallery flyers, then taught a generation at CalArts.

principles.name: Use every tool at once
principles.idea: Found type, Letraset, stencils, scribble, clip art and the photostat sit together on one page.
principles.example: Detroit Focus Gallery poster, Morris Brose: A Sustained Vision, 1987

principles.name: Make every letter different
principles.idea: A sans serif is redrawn by hand with varying weights, curves and tails so no two characters repeat.

principles.name: After the fact
principles.idea: Posters made for those who attended an event, not to sell it beforehand, free the work from commercial persuasion.

keyWorks.title: Detroit Focus Gallery poster, Morris Brose: A Sustained Vision

figures.name: Bruce Tognazzini
figures.summary: Apple's first applications engineer; wrote the first Apple Human Interface Guidelines and later partnered in Nielsen Norman Group.

principles.name: The guideline as contract
principles.idea: Consistency across applications is a promise to users, so write it down and enforce it.
principles.example: Apple Human Interface Guidelines, first edition (Apple II), 1978

principles.name: Fitts's law at the edge
principles.idea: Targets at the screen edge are effectively infinite in depth, so put the most-used commands there.
principles.example: The Macintosh menu bar pinned to the top edge, 1984

principles.name: First principles over fashion
principles.idea: Ground interaction in durable principles (anticipation, latency reduction, visible state) rather than look.

keyWorks.title: Human Interface Guidelines: The Apple Desktop Interface

figures.name: Mohieddine Ellabbad
figures.summary: Egyptian illustrator-designer who built a modern Arab children's book culture through Dar al-Fata al-Arabi and books about images.

principles.name: Visual literacy for the reader
principles.idea: Books about images, written and designed by the designer.

principles.name: Memory as material
principles.idea: Visual memories addressed across generations.

principles.name: Arab publishing for Arab children
principles.idea: Build the publisher, not only the pages.

figures.name: Katherine McCoy
figures.summary: Co-chair of Cranbrook's design programme from 1971 to 1995, who joined Unimark-trained rigour to vernacular, semiotics and deconstruction.

principles.name: Layered reading
principles.idea: Visual and verbal readings overlap so a poster offers several routes in rather than one hierarchy.
principles.example: Cranbrook Graduate Program in Design poster, 1989

principles.name: Studio as laboratory
principles.idea: Minimal assignments and weekly critiques let each student develop a personal design voice, balanced by real client work.

principles.name: Read deeply, then design
principles.idea: Students read history and theory behind their concerns and design with those ideas, from Venturi to post-structuralism.

keyWorks.title: Cranbrook Graduate Program in Design poster

figures.name: Vaughan Oliver
figures.summary: 4AD's designer (23 Envelope, then v23), whose surreal, tactile photography and ornate type gave a whole record label one atmosphere.

principles.name: Label as one atmosphere
principles.idea: Different bands share one visual sensibility, so the label itself becomes the brand.

principles.name: Continuity with a fresh approach
principles.idea: Each release of a band's catalogue is new but recognisably part of a series.

principles.name: Texture and the uncanny
principles.idea: Close-up photography, blur and surreal objects make the image felt before it is understood.

figures.name: Alan Chan
figures.role: Graphic and interior designer, brand consultant
figures.summary: Hong Kong brand designer whose 'East meets West' blend of Chinese ornament and Western layout reached Japan and the mainland first.

principles.name: East meets West
principles.idea: Chinese decorative vocabulary set in Western layouts for consumer brands.
principles.example: East Meets West exhibition, Creation Gallery G8, Tokyo, 1991

principles.name: Nostalgia as brand asset
principles.idea: Old Shanghai graphics reissued as products and packaging.
principles.example: Alan Chan Design Company retro products, 1990s

keyWorks.title: Art of Living (Hong Kong Heritage Museum)

figures.name: Tibor Kalman
figures.summary: Founder of M&Co and editor of Benetton's Colors, the 'bad boy' who used vernacular graphics and provocation as design's conscience.

principles.name: Vernacular against corporate
principles.idea: The language of cheap signs, menus and diners is used as a protest against corporate International Style.

principles.name: Good design needs a good client
principles.idea: Design is only good if it serves an ethical end and increases public awareness.

principles.name: Provoke with the obvious
principles.idea: A single doctored image, the Queen recast as Black, says more than an essay.
principles.example: Colors issue on race with doctored portraits, 1993

keyWorks.title: Talking Heads, Remain in Light (with the band)

figures.name: David Carson
figures.summary: A former pro surfer whose layouts for Beach Culture and Ray Gun made intuitive, layered, barely legible typography a mainstream style.

principles.name: Don't mistake legibility for communication
principles.idea: A page that is hard to read can still communicate, through texture and emotion, if it is honest to its content.

principles.name: Basic decisions make the work
principles.idea: Image choice, cropping and type choice matter more than the software's ability to overlap or fade.

principles.name: Each page its own answer
principles.idea: No template: every spread is resolved from scratch by intuition.

keyWorks.title: Nine Inch Nails, The Fragile packaging

figures.name: Pentagram
figures.summary: Partnership of equals founded in London in 1972; its New York office (1978) became the main heir of New York School wit in identity design.

principles.name: A partnership of designers
principles.idea: Each partner leads their own clients and team; profits are shared equally.

principles.name: The idea, again
principles.idea: Wit and concept carried from Fletcher/Forbes/Gill into identity work.

principles.name: Identity as voice
principles.idea: Typography and tone carry a brand as much as a logo does.
principles.example: Michael Bierut, Saks Fifth Avenue identity, 2007

figures.name: Paula Scher
figures.summary: From CBS Records covers to Pentagram's Public Theater identity, she spoke new things in the borrowed grammar of Constructivism and wood type.

principles.name: Historical vocabulary, not historical copy
principles.idea: Borrow the grammar of Constructivism or Deco and say something new with it.
principles.example: The Best of Jazz poster, CBS Records, 1979

principles.name: Parody as homage
principles.idea: Reprise a classic so precisely the reference becomes the message.

principles.name: Type as the street
principles.idea: Loud, mixed wood type that feels like the city an institution lives in.

figures.name: Kamal Boullata
figures.summary: Palestinian artist-historian whose Kufic-on-the-square silkscreens bridged icon and Islamic geometry; author of the standard history of Palestinian art.

principles.name: The square as root
principles.idea: Two intersecting squares in a circle unite star, mandorla and Jerusalem's sacred plans.

principles.name: Write the image
principles.idea: From icon painting: the iconographer writes rather than paints.

principles.name: Stencil precision
principles.idea: Pochoir and silkscreen give crisp, measured flat colour.

figures.name: Dan Friedman
figures.summary: Ulm- and Basel-trained designer and teacher who carried Weingart's ideas into American classrooms and argued for a 'radical modernism'.

principles.name: Readability, not legibility
principles.idea: He replaced legibility, a property of letters, with readability, whether a whole piece invites reading.

principles.name: Radical modernism
principles.idea: Keep modernism's social optimism but drop its puritan restraint, letting in colour, kitsch and the personal.

principles.name: No border between disciplines
principles.idea: Corporate identity, Day-Glo furniture and art catalogues are one practice.

figures.name: Muriel Cooper
figures.role: Book designer, digital design researcher, educator
figures.summary: MIT Press design director turned founder of the Visible Language Workshop, whose 1994 Information Landscapes put typography into navigable 3D space.

principles.name: Information as landscape
principles.idea: Hierarchy can be spatial depth and focus rather than page order; the reader flies through text.

principles.name: Designers must build the tools
principles.idea: If design moves onto screens, designers have to work inside the computer, not hand off to engineers.
principles.example: Visible Language Workshop, MIT, from the mid-1970s

principles.name: Modernist rigour, radical variation
principles.idea: Bauhaus discipline can be pushed into new forms rather than repeated.
principles.example: Learning from Las Vegas, first edition design, MIT Press, 1972

figures.name: The Designers Republic
figures.role: Graphic design studio (Ian Anderson, Nick Phillips)
figures.summary: Sheffield studio that parodied corporate identity and consumerism for Warp Records, Pop Will Eat Itself and the Wipeout games.

principles.name: Brand the anti-brand
principles.idea: Corporate logos, slogans and fake company names are turned on consumerism itself.
principles.example: 'Work Buy Consume Die' slogans; Pho-Ku corporation, 1990s

principles.name: Maximum-minimalism
principles.idea: Clean, technical layouts are overloaded with icons, codes, anime and tiny type until restraint becomes excess.

principles.name: North of Nowhere
principles.idea: Regional pride (Sheffield, 'SoYo') against the London design scene is part of the voice.

figures.name: Irma Boom
figures.summary: Amsterdam book designer who builds books as architecture: 2,136 pages without page numbers, inkless embossed pages, sawn edges.

principles.name: Build the book
principles.idea: Thickness, edges, scale and binding carry the content; she works out each book first as a tiny model.

principles.name: Remove the expected
principles.idea: No page numbers, no index, a blank cover, reverse chronology, so the reader discovers rather than navigates.

principles.name: Address other senses
principles.idea: Embossing without ink or frayed edges speak to touch where print would speak to sight.

keyWorks.title: Irma Boom: The Architecture of the Book

figures.name: Jony Ive
figures.summary: Apple's industrial design chief from the iMac to the iPhone, who took over software design and led the flat redesign of iOS 7.

principles.name: Simplicity is order
principles.idea: Simplicity is not absence of ornament but bringing order to complexity.

principles.name: Deference to content
principles.idea: The interface should step back so content and the user's task lead.
principles.example: iOS 7 translucent bars and borderless buttons, 2013

principles.name: Materials lead form
principles.idea: Form follows how a material is worked (polycarbonate, aluminium unibody, glass).
principles.example: iMac G3 translucent Bondi Blue polycarbonate, 1998

figures.summary: Sugiura-trained Beijing designer who moved Chinese practice from cover decoration to book design as a whole object.

principles.idea: Text, grid, paper and binding form one structure, starting from the body text.

principles.name: Material as meaning
principles.idea: Wood, thread, rice paper and traditional binding used as structural argument, not decoration.

figures.summary: An M&Co alumnus whose handmade, often bodily typography for music and his own lectures made the designer's life part of the content.

principles.idea: Lettering is cut, built or written physically, so the labour and risk of making show.

figures.summary: MIT Media Lab professor, RISD president and tech-industry design executive who argued designers must code and later that they must understand AI.

principles.name: Learn the material by coding
principles.idea: Designers should write simple programs to understand the computer as a medium.

principles.name: Laws of simplicity
principles.idea: Reduce, organise, save time; simplicity is subtracting the obvious and adding the meaningful.

principles.name: Computational design as a business force
principles.idea: Track design's shift into technology companies and name computational design as its own category.

figures.name: Takashi Murakami
figures.summary: Coined Superflat and ran it as a brand system across painting, merchandise, Louis Vuitton and Kanye West covers.

principles.name: The art enterprise
principles.idea: The studio as a company with production lines, like an animation house.

principles.name: Repackage the subcultural
principles.idea: Otaku forms presented as high art and sold back as goods.

principles.name: Curate your own context
principles.idea: Theory, exhibitions and product built together.

figures.name: Huda Smitshuijzen AbiFarès
figures.summary: Author of Arabic Typography (2001) and founder of the Khatt Foundation (2004), the research and matchmaking hub of bilingual Arabic type.

principles.name: Structure before style
principles.idea: Analyse Arabic typography structurally and theoretically.

principles.name: Matchmaking
principles.idea: Pair Arabic and Latin designers to make genuinely bilingual families.

principles.name: Build the library
principles.idea: Publish the region's design history.

figures.name: Norm

figures.summary: Zurich duo who rebuilt Swiss modernism from its rules, producing strict, slightly strange typefaces such as Simple and Replica for Lineto.

principles.idea: A typeface comes from a stated construction system, so its oddities are the system's, not the hand's.

principles.name: Modernism with a wink
principles.idea: Strict, rigorous Swiss method with slight references to postmodern play.

figures.name: Joshua Davis
figures.summary: Flash-era designer whose praystation.com won the 2001 Golden Nica and who opened his source files to a generation.

principles.name: Program the composition
principles.idea: Write rules and let randomness compose within them; the output is a family, not a single image.

principles.name: Give away the source
principles.idea: Publishing working files builds a community that learns and remixes.
principles.example: praystation.com, one of the first sites to publish its Flash source files, 2001

figures.name: Jonathan Barnbrook
figures.summary: Type designer and activist who gives fonts provocative names, uses détournement against corporations, and designed Bowie's late sleeves.

principles.name: Design as a weapon
principles.idea: Graphic work is a political response, often parodying advertising's own language.
principles.example: Billboard 'Designers, stay away from corporations that want you to lie for them', 2001

principles.name: The loaded typeface
principles.idea: A font's name and its historical form (blackletter, inscription) carry an argument.

principles.name: Type as the cover
principles.idea: A bespoke typeface does the work of the image on a record sleeve.

figures.name: Kenya Hara
figures.summary: Muji's art director since 2001 and NDC's president, who theorised emptiness, white and ex-formation as design.

principles.name: Emptiness
principles.idea: Design as an empty vessel that receives meaning rather than sending a message.

principles.name: Ex-formation
principles.idea: Make the familiar unknown again so people notice it, instead of informing them.
principles.example: Ex-formation seminar at Musashino Art University, from 2004

principles.name: Haptic design
principles.idea: Design addressed to touch and the senses before the eye.

figures.name: Kashiwa Sato
figures.summary: Founder of SAMURAI, whose loud reduction in primary colours shaped Uniqlo, Seven-Eleven, Rakuten and the National Art Center, Tokyo.

principles.name: Organising
principles.idea: Branding as tidying: find the essence and discard the rest.

principles.name: Reduction, loudly
principles.idea: Straight lines, primary colours and one strong square.

principles.name: Brand as environment
principles.idea: Logo, store, product and architecture directed as one.

figures.name: Reza Abedini

principles.name: The letter as aesthetic and concept
principles.idea: Persian script carries the idea, not just the caption.

principles.name: Reread the heritage, don't quote it
