principles.name: Look at the world
principles.idea: Ground interface forms in everyday objects; if the world is full of a shape, the screen should be able to draw it.
principles.example: Insisting on QuickDraw round rectangles, May 1981

principles.name: Typography belongs in computing
principles.idea: Proportional, beautiful type is a requirement, not a luxury, traced by Jobs to a calligraphy class.

principles.name: Integrate and edit
principles.idea: Own hardware and software together and cut ruthlessly so the product feels like one thing.
principles.example: iPhone with multi-touch and no hardware keyboard, 2007

figures.name: Scott Forstall
figures.summary: Led iPhone software from its creation until 2012 and was widely reported as the leading internal advocate of skeuomorphic iOS.

principles.name: Familiarity first
principles.idea: New users on a new device learn faster when apps look like the objects they replace.
principles.example: iPhone OS 1.0 Notes, Calculator and Clock apps, 2007

principles.name: The platform is the product
principles.idea: Open the device to third-party apps under shared rules and frameworks.

figures.name: Yugo Nakamura
figures.summary: Tokyo designer trained in engineering whose physics-driven Flash interfaces and UNIQLOCK defined interactive craft in the 2000s.

principles.name: Behaviour modelled on nature
principles.idea: Use the maths of natural motion (springs, growth, flow) so interaction feels familiar without instruction.

principles.name: Loop as experience
principles.idea: A perpetual, music-timed loop turns a utility (a clock) into a brand ritual.

figures.name: Albert Shum
figures.summary: Led the Microsoft design team behind Windows Phone 7, the first mass-market phone interface built on Metro's typographic flatness.

principles.name: Authentically digital
principles.idea: Drop simulated materials; let typography, colour and motion native to the screen do the work.

principles.name: Signage, not simulation
principles.idea: Borrow from transit wayfinding: big type, flat colour fields, immediate legibility.

figures.name: Ethan Marcotte
figures.summary: Coined 'responsive web design' in 2010 and defined it as fluid grids, flexible images and media queries.

principles.name: One design, many facets
principles.idea: Treat every device as a facet of a single experience rather than building separate sites.
principles.example: Responsive Web Design, A List Apart, 2010

principles.name: Proportion over pixels
principles.idea: Express the grid as ratios (target over context equals result) so layout scales.

principles.name: Learn from architecture
principles.idea: Borrow responsive architecture's idea that structure and inhabitant shape each other.
principles.example: Responsive Web Design, A List Apart, 2010

keyWorks.title: The Boston Globe website (with Filament Group)

figures.name: Why Not Associates
figures.role: Graphic design studio (Andy Altmann, David Ellis)
figures.summary: London studio that took 1980s experimental typography into motion, exhibitions and public space, ending up with type you can walk on.

principles.name: Type at architectural scale
principles.idea: Typography leaves the page and becomes floor, wall and landscape, readable from close up and from a tower.
principles.example: Comedy Carpet, Blackpool, with Gordon Young, 2011

principles.name: Experiment for clients
principles.idea: Layered, kinetic typography is applied to commissions rather than kept to self-initiated work.

figures.name: Loren Brichter
figures.summary: Independent developer who invented pull-to-refresh and whose flat, colour-coded Letterpress anticipated iOS 7.

principles.name: The gesture is the button
principles.idea: Fold a command into the natural motion of the content so no control is needed.

principles.name: Colour as state
principles.idea: Flat fields of colour can encode game state and ownership more clearly than texture.

figures.name: Bret Victor
figures.summary: Former Apple human-interface inventor whose essays and talks argue for immediate, explorable, physical computing; founder of Dynamicland.

principles.name: Immediate connection
principles.idea: Creators need to see the effect of every change instantly; latency between thought and result kills ideas.

principles.name: Information software is graphic design
principles.idea: Most software is for learning, not doing, so its core problem is showing data, not adding interaction.

principles.name: Beyond pictures under glass
principles.idea: Hands do far more than tap glass; the future interface should use the body and physical space.
principles.example: A Brief Rant on the Future of Interaction Design, 2011

keyWorks.title: A Brief Rant on the Future of Interaction Design

figures.name: Experimental Jetset
figures.role: Graphic design studio (Danny van den Dungen, Marieke Stolk, Erwin Brinkers)
figures.summary: Amsterdam trio who fused Dutch modernism with post-punk attitude, using Helvetica, black, white, red and blue as a critical, not corporate, language.

principles.name: Restricted means
principles.idea: Typography alone, mostly Helvetica, in black, white, red and blue: the limits are the identity.

principles.name: Modernism plus punk
principles.idea: De Stijl and Provo are read through Sonic Youth: modernism as an attitude of making, not a corporate look.
principles.example: Studio name, after Sonic Youth's Experimental Jet Set, Trash and No Star (1994), 1997

principles.name: A line that responds
principles.idea: An identity is a single rule that scales to whatever format it lands in.

keyWorks.title: Statement and Counter-Statement: Notes on Experimental Jetset

figures.name: Brad Frost
figures.summary: Wrote Atomic Design (2013 post, 2016 book), the most influential method for building interface design systems.

principles.name: Atoms to pages
principles.idea: Build interfaces from atoms, molecules, organisms, templates and pages, moving between abstract parts and concrete screens.

principles.name: A living pattern library
principles.idea: Keep the components in a working, browsable environment that is the real code, not a static PDF.

principles.name: Maintain it like a product
principles.idea: A design system needs people, process and governance to survive past launch.

figures.name: Aaron Nieh
figures.summary: Taiwan's best-known graphic designer: Mandopop packaging, sliced Chinese typography and crowdfunded civic design, first Taiwanese AGI member.

principles.name: Characters as malleable material
principles.idea: Chinese characters sliced, layered and distorted until they are image and text at once.

principles.name: Design as civic action
principles.idea: Crowdfunded political design placed in mass media.

figures.name: Matías Duarte
figures.summary: Designed Danger's Sidekick and Palm's webOS, then led Android and Material Design at Google.

principles.name: Cards for multitasking
principles.idea: Running apps as physical-feeling cards you flick away makes concurrency graspable.

principles.name: A material, not an imitation
principles.idea: Invent one consistent material with its own physics instead of copying leather and wood.

principles.name: Between literal and abstract
principles.idea: Avoid both heavy skeuomorphism and austere signage; Android's Holo was framed against both.

images.title: Android 5 Lollipop
images.credit: Google LLC, The Android Open Source Project

figures.name: Alan Dye
figures.summary: Head of Apple's Human Interface design from 2015, who led Liquid Glass before leaving for Meta in December 2025.

principles.name: Interface as material
principles.idea: Treat UI as a physical material with its own optics and behaviour, not as flat graphics.

principles.name: Hardware and software as one shape
principles.idea: Let the interface adopt and even disguise the hardware's form.

events.label: Chromolithography patented
events.note: Godefroy Engelmann's patent for printing colour from multiple stones made mass colour printing, and later the colour poster, possible.

events.label: Great Exhibition, London
events.note: The Crystal Palace displayed industrial goods so overdecorated that it provoked the design-reform movement, from Owen Jones to Morris.

events.label: The Grammar of Ornament
events.note: Owen Jones's chromolithographed survey made ornament a teachable system and became the period's standard pattern source.

events.label: Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. founded
events.note: A firm where designers made what they designed: the practical start of the Arts and Crafts movement.

events.label: Edmund Evans colour toy books
events.note: Evans's colour wood-engraved picture books with Walter Crane made the illustrated children's book a designed object for a mass market.

events.label: Exposition Universelle, Paris
events.note: Japan's display of prints and crafts fed the Japonisme that reshaped Western poster composition.

events.label: Prang's Christmas cards
events.note: Louis Prang's chromolithographed cards brought high-quality colour printing into ordinary American homes.

events.label: First halftone photograph in a newspaper
events.note: The New York Daily Graphic printed A Scene in Shantytown, beginning the replacement of hand engraving by photographic reproduction.

events.label: French press law of 29 July
events.note: Liberalised bill-posting in France, opening Paris's walls to the colour poster boom of the 1880s and 1890s.

events.label: Ives halftone process patented
events.note: Frederic Ives's screen method made photographs printable alongside type in ordinary letterpress.

events.label: Linotype
events.note: Ottmar Mergenthaler's line-casting machine went into use at the New York Tribune, mechanising text composition for newspapers and books.

events.label: Monotype
events.note: Tolbert Lanston founded the company behind the single-type caster that brought hot-metal quality to book typesetting and later commissioned historic revivals.

events.label: Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society founded
events.note: Gave the movement its name and a public showcase in London, with Walter Crane as founding president.

events.label: Kelmscott Press founded
events.note: William Morris's press launched the private press revival and reset standards for type, paper and page design.

events.label: Maison de l'Art Nouveau opens
events.note: Siegfried Bing's Paris gallery gave the international style its name.

events.label: Jugend founded
events.note: Georg Hirth's Munich weekly gave German Art Nouveau its name, Jugendstil, and a cover a week to experiment on.

events.label: Vienna Secession founded
events.note: Klimt, Moser, Hoffmann and Olbrich broke with the academy and launched a design language that turned the curve into the square.

events.label: Exposition Universelle, Paris
events.note: The high point and public consecration of Art Nouveau, with Guimard's Métro entrances opening the same year.

events.label: Wiener Werkstätte founded
events.note: Hoffmann, Moser and Fritz Waerndorfer's workshop applied a single geometric language to every object and stamped each with makers' marks.

events.label: Offset lithography on paper
events.note: Ira Washington Rubel's offset press transferred the image via a rubber blanket, the process that would come to dominate commercial printing.

events.label: Die Brücke founded in Dresden
events.note: The Expressionist group revived the woodcut as a raw modern medium, the starting point the Bauhaus later left behind.

events.label: Deutscher Werkbund founded; Behrens joins AEG
events.note: Industry, artists and the state allied to raise German product quality, and AEG hired Behrens to design its whole identity.

events.label: Manifesto of Futurism
events.note: Marinetti's front-page manifesto in Le Figaro made the manifesto itself the avant-garde's primary design medium.

events.label: Das Plakat magazine
events.note: The Verein der Plakatfreunde's journal treated posters as collectible art and documented Plakatstil as it happened.

events.label: Werkbund exhibition, Cologne; First World War
events.note: The Muthesius-van de Velde debate on standard types versus artistic individuality, then the war, closed the ornament era.

events.label: Zang Tumb Tuuum published
events.note: Marinetti's words-in-freedom book broke the horizontal line and made typography perform sound.

events.label: BLAST no. 1
events.note: Vorticism's magenta magazine turned heavy grotesque type and lists into polemic layout.

events.label: 0,10 exhibition and Black Square
events.note: Malevich launched Suprematism in Petrograd, giving later design a grammar of floating geometric planes.

events.label: Cabaret Voltaire opens in Zurich
events.note: The birthplace of Dada, whose collage and typographic anarchy fed photomontage and the New Typography.

events.label: Johnston's Underground alphabet
events.note: Edward Johnston's sans for London Underground became the template for corporate typefaces and Gill Sans.

events.label: De Stijl magazine founded
events.note: Van Doesburg's journal spread Neo-Plasticism's grid, primaries and rectangular letters across Europe.

events.label: October Revolution
events.note: The Bolshevik state recast artists as constructors of a new society, creating Constructivist graphic design.

events.label: Bauhaus founded in Weimar
events.note: Gropius merged art academy and craft school into the model for modern design education.

events.label: First International Dada Fair, Berlin
events.note: The high point of Berlin Dada put photomontage and political collage in front of the public.

events.label: Devětsil founded in Prague
events.note: The Czech avant-garde union that produced Poetism, the picture poem and Teige's typography.

events.label: First Working Group of Constructivists
events.note: Rodchenko, Stepanova and Gan rejected easel painting for production art at INKhUK in Moscow.

events.label: DIN 476 paper sizes
events.note: Germany's A-series standard gave the New Typography its formats for letterheads, posters and forms.

events.label: First Russian Art Exhibition, Berlin
events.note: Galerie van Diemen's show brought Suprematism and Constructivism to Western European designers.

events.label: Bauhaus exhibition, Weimar
events.note: Under the slogan Art and Technology, a New Unity, the Bauhaus turned from craft Expressionism toward industry.

events.label: Bauhaus moves to Dessau
events.note: The Dessau years produced the school's printing workshop, Bayer's universal and its mature graphic style.

events.label: Exposition internationale des arts décoratifs, Paris
events.note: The exhibition gave Art Deco its name and showcased Cassandre, Melnikov and Rodchenko's Workers' Club.

events.label: elementare typographie
events.note: Tschichold's special issue of a trade journal brought avant-garde typography to ordinary compositors.

events.label: Abeceda published
events.note: Nezval, Teige and Mayerová stage the alphabet as dance and photomontage, a landmark of avant-garde book typography.

events.label: Futura released
events.note: Renner's geometric sans, sold by Bauer as the typeface of our time, became modernism's default voice.

events.label: Die neue Typographie published
events.note: Tschichold's handbook codified asymmetry, sans serif and standard formats as rules for designers.

events.label: Pressa, Cologne
events.note: Lissitzky's Soviet pavilion set the standard for immersive exhibition design with photomontage.

events.label: Shanghai Sketch launched
events.note: Zhang Guangyu's weekly began Shanghai's manhua golden age, the testing ground for Chinese modernist graphics.

events.label: Film und Foto, Stuttgart
events.note: The Werkbund show made the New Vision photography central to modern graphic design.

events.label: Teige lectures at the Bauhaus
events.note: Prague's leading theorist teaches in Dessau, linking Czech Poetism to the Bauhaus.

events.label: Soviet decree dissolves artistic groups
events.note: The 23 April decree ended independent avant-garde groups, clearing the way for Socialist Realism in 1934.

events.label: Bauhaus closes
events.note: Nazi pressure closed the school in Berlin, scattering its teachers to the USA, Britain and Switzerland.

events.label: Beck's London Underground map
events.note: Harry Beck's diagram, drawn like a circuit with only verticals, horizontals and 45 degree lines, founded the topological transit map.

events.label: Nippon Kobo founded
events.note: Natori's studio trained Hiromu Hara and Yusaku Kamekura in modern photo-typographic layout.

events.label: Brodovitch joins Harper's Bazaar
events.note: European avant-garde layout enters the American mass-market magazine.

events.label: New Bauhaus opens in Chicago
events.note: Moholy-Nagy transplants Bauhaus teaching to the US, backed by Walter Paepcke's circle.

events.label: Degenerate Art exhibition, Munich
events.note: The Nazis mocked modern art publicly, confirming the exile of the German avant-garde.

events.label: Taller de Gráfica Popular founded
events.note: Leopoldo Méndez, Pablo O'Higgins and Luis Arenal found the Mexico City print collective, making the linocut a mass political medium.

events.label: MoMA's Bauhaus 1919–1928 exhibition
events.note: Gives émigré modernism institutional standing in America.

events.label: Sutnar stays in New York
events.note: After the Nazi occupation the Czech avant-garde typographer remains in the US and goes on to found American information design.

events.label: Unified Arabic patented
events.note: Nasri Khattar's one-form-per-letter Arabic print script cuts the glyph set to 33 for machine typesetting.

events.label: Polish posters win in Vienna
events.note: Tomaszewski's five first prizes start international attention to the Polish poster.

events.label: Madiha Omar's calligraphic paintings shown in Washington
events.note: Generally taken as the first exhibition of modern art built from Arabic letters, the start of hurufiyya.

events.label: Die gute Form exhibition
events.note: Max Bill's Swiss Werkbund show turned 'good form' into a public argument for everyday design.

events.label: CCA Great Ideas of Western Man
events.note: Container Corporation's campaign proves enlightened corporate patronage of designers.

events.label: International Design Conference in Aspen
events.note: Walter Paepcke's conference links designers and business leaders for decades.

events.label: CBS eye
events.note: William Golden shows a single symbol can carry a brand on television.

events.label: Japan Advertising Artists Club (Nissenbi)
events.note: Japan's first professional body for graphic designers, and its exhibitions launched Awazu, Sugiura and Yokoo.

events.label: First Bienal de São Paulo
events.note: Max Bill's prize and his MASP retrospective the same year ignite Brazilian concrete art and, through it, Brazilian modern design.

events.label: Sindbad magazine launched in Cairo
events.note: Hussein Bicar's Sindbad, Egypt's first children's magazine, trained a generation of Arab illustrators.

events.label: Olivetti: Design in Industry at MoMA
events.note: Made Olivetti the world's model of a company whose identity is everything it makes.

events.label: HfG Ulm founded
events.note: The post-war successor to the Bauhaus, where design became science, semiotics and systems.

events.label: First Compasso d'Oro
events.note: Italy's design prize, first won by Nizzoli's Lettera 22, put industrial design on the cultural map.

events.label: The Man with the Golden Arm titles
events.note: Saul Bass makes the film title sequence a designed prologue.

events.label: Graphic '55 exhibition, Tokyo
events.note: Japanese modernists hung beside Paul Rand at Takashimaya, inspiring the generation that founded NDC.

events.label: IBM logo and design programme
events.note: Rand's mark and Eliot Noyes's total design programme set the template for corporate identity.

events.label: PRC newspapers switch to horizontal setting
events.note: On 1 January 1956 every newspaper in the People's Republic moved from vertical to horizontal typesetting by decree.

events.label: Projekt magazine founded in Warsaw
events.note: The design magazine of the Polish thaw, co-designed by Cieślewicz, carried the school abroad.

events.label: Braun SK 4
events.note: Gugelot and Rams' radio-phonograph replaced the wooden cabinet with a rational appliance.

events.label: Neue Haas Grotesk (Helvetica)
events.note: Miedinger and Hoffmann's neo-grotesque, renamed Helvetica in 1960, became modernism's default voice.

events.label: Univers
events.note: Frutiger's family, made for Lumitype phototypesetting, introduced the numbered weight-and-width system.

events.label: Neue Grafik magazine
events.note: The trilingual Zürich quarterly (1958-65) that served as the Swiss Style's manifesto.

events.label: Think Small (Volkswagen)
events.note: DDB's ad crowns the Creative Revolution's idea-first, art-director-plus-copywriter method.

events.label: Cuban Revolution
events.note: ICAIC is founded in March 1959, and with advertising gone the poster becomes a cultural rather than commercial medium.

events.label: Chase Manhattan octagon
events.note: One of the first purely abstract American corporate symbols.

events.label: World Design Conference, Tokyo
events.note: Held 11-16 May with 227 delegates; it put Japanese design on the world stage and launched the Metabolist manifesto.

events.label: Nippon Design Center opens
events.note: Eight corporations funded a shared design department led by Kamekura, Hara and Tanaka.

events.label: Brasília inaugurated
events.note: Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer's capital, opened 21 April 1960, makes modernism Brazil's official national image.

events.label: Letraset dry-transfer lettering
events.note: Rub-down letters put display type in anyone's hands, the tool of choice for punk fanzines and the vernacular postmodernists.

events.label: Lufthansa identity
events.note: Otl Aicher's Ulm group delivered one of the first complete corporate identity systems with a manual.

events.label: ESDI opens in Rio de Janeiro
events.note: Latin America's first university-level design school, built on the Ulm model with Wollner, Magalhães and Bergmiller among its founders.

events.label: Sketchpad
events.note: Ivan Sutherland's light-pen drawing program introduced direct graphical manipulation and constraints, the seed of CAD and of every drawing tool since.

events.label: Total Design founded
events.note: The Netherlands' first multidisciplinary design consultancy, bringing total identity to public life.

events.label: Tokyo 1964 Olympics design programme
events.note: Kamekura's emblem and photo posters and the first systematic Olympic pictograms set the template for event identity.

events.label: First Things First manifesto
events.note: Ken Garland's manifesto asked designers to prefer useful communication to consumer advertising, a question every later generation reopened.

events.label: Designing Programmes
events.note: Karl Gerstner reframed design as writing rules that generate solutions, a root of parametric design.

events.label: Unimark International founded
events.note: Systems modernism is industrialised as a corporate design firm.

events.label: Persona exhibition, Matsuya Ginza
events.note: Sixteen young designers, including Yokoo with his hanged self-portrait, announced the break with corporate modernism.

events.label: Kanoon founded in Tehran
events.note: The children's institute became the laboratory of Iranian illustration, animation and graphic design.

events.label: Cultural Revolution begins
events.note: Propaganda posters reached their peak production and the most centralised image-making in design history.

events.label: First International Poster Biennale, Warsaw
events.note: The world's first recurring event devoted to the poster.

events.label: Tricontinental Conference, Havana
events.note: Founds OSPAAAL, whose multilingual solidarity posters, folded into Tricontinental magazine, become a graphic network for the Global South.

events.label: First Shiraz Arts Festival
events.note: An annual international festival (1967–1977) whose posters and programmes were key commissions for Iranian designers.

events.label: Summer of Love
events.note: San Francisco's counterculture turned the dance-hall poster into a national craze and a collectible product.

events.label: New Alphabet
events.note: Wim Crouwel's type for cathode-ray screens treated the display's limits as the design brief.

events.label: Poster Museum at Wilanów opens
events.note: The world's first museum dedicated to the poster.

events.label: Mexico 68 Olympics and Tlatelolco
events.note: The most complete Olympic identity yet opens days after the 2 October massacre; protesters answer with a bayonet-pierced dove.

events.label: The Mother of All Demos
events.note: Engelbart's 9 December demo showed the mouse, windows, hypertext and live collaboration in one system.

events.label: HfG Ulm closes
events.note: Funding cuts and conflict ended the school, scattering the Ulm Model across the world.

events.label: Mexico City Metro opens
events.note: Line 1 opens on 4-5 September 1969 with Lance Wyman's station pictograms, a wayfinding system designed for every literacy level.

events.label: NYCTA Graphics Standards Manual
events.note: Vignelli and Noorda's manual makes Helvetica the voice of the New York subway.

events.label: International Typeface Corporation founded
events.note: Lubalin, Burns and Rondthaler license phototype faces, spreading expressive display type.

events.label: Expo '70, Osaka
events.note: Over 64 million visitors; Japanese graphic and architectural avant-gardes worked at national scale on pavilions and signs.

events.label: Polish poster designers teach in Havana
events.note: Górka and Świerzy lead workshops in Cuba, linking the Polish and Cuban poster schools.

events.label: Instituto Di Tella closes its art centres
events.note: Under the Onganía regime the Buenos Aires avant-garde's home, and Argentina's first professional design department, close in 1970.

events.label: One Dimension Group manifesto
events.note: Shakir Hassan Al Said's Baghdad manifesto gives hurufiyya its most articulate theory.

events.label: Federal Design Improvement Program
events.note: After Nixon's memo, the NEA brings modernist identity and graphics standards to US federal agencies.

events.label: Vignelli New York City Subway diagram
events.note: Diagram over geography becomes the defining argument in transit cartography.

events.label: IBM eight-bar logo
events.note: Rand's striped revision becomes one of the most recognised corporate marks.

events.label: Pentagram founded
events.note: A partnership of equal designer-owners becomes a new model for the design firm.

events.label: Korea Society of Graphic Design founded
events.note: Korea's first graphic design association, later KSVD, institutionalised the profession.

events.label: Learning from Las Vegas
events.note: Venturi, Scott Brown and Izenour's book licensed the commercial vernacular as a source, shaping Cranbrook and postmodern graphics.

events.label: Dynabook proposal
events.note: Alan Kay's paper imagined a personal, portable computer for learning, a blueprint for the laptop and tablet.

events.label: Munich Olympics identity
events.note: Otl Aicher's grid pictograms and light palette set the template for wayfinding and event identity.

events.label: Chilean coup
events.note: The 11 September coup ends Allende's government, painting over Unidad Popular murals and scattering its designers into exile.

events.label: Xerox Alto
events.note: The first workstation with a bitmapped display, mouse and graphical interface, built at PARC.

events.label: AIGA/DOT Symbol Signs
events.note: 34 public pictograms set the standard for US wayfinding.

events.label: Dar al-Fata al-Arabi founded
events.note: A Beirut-based Arab children's publisher, co-founded by Ellabbad, that built a regional visual culture for young readers.

events.label: NASA worm logotype
events.note: Danne & Blackburn's mark, under the federal program, is the high point of public-sector modernism.

events.label: I♥NY
events.note: Milton Glaser's rebus shows a mark can change how people feel about a place.

events.label: National Park Service Unigrid
events.note: Vignelli's grid standardises every US national park brochure.

events.label: Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art opens
events.note: Kamran Diba's museum showed Iranian modernists beside a major Western collection, two years before the revolution.

events.label: Punk's year
events.note: 'God Save the Queen' and Never Mind the Bollocks made cut-up, photocopied graphics a mass-market look.

events.label: Pentagram opens in New York
events.note: Carries London wit into American identity design; later home of Scher and Bierut.

events.label: JAGDA founded
events.note: The Japan Graphic Designers Association formed with Kamekura as first president.

events.label: Iranian Revolution
events.note: Ends royal cultural patronage and makes the political and martyrdom poster Iran's dominant public genre.

events.label: Apple visits Xerox PARC
events.note: Jobs and Apple engineers saw the Alto's interface, which shaped the Lisa and Macintosh.

events.label: Muji launched
events.note: Forty no-brand products from Seiyu, designed by Ikko Tanaka's team, began the design of emptiness.

events.label: Memphis founded in Milan
events.note: Sottsass's group launched postmodern design's loudest attack on functionalist good taste; its first show followed in 1981.

events.label: Xerox Star 8010
events.note: The first commercial computer sold with a desktop of icons, folders and a mouse.

events.label: Grid Systems in Graphic Design
events.note: Müller-Brockmann codified the modular grid in the book still used to teach layout.

events.label: Hiroshima Appeals poster series begins
events.note: JAGDA's annual peace poster, opened by Kamekura's Burning Butterflies, became a lasting commission for Japanese designers.

events.label: Apple Lisa
events.note: The first mass-market GUI computer, launched 19 January at US$9,995.

events.label: Apple Macintosh
events.note: A bitmap screen, mouse and fonts on a desk made type and layout a personal, experimental medium; Emigre launched the same year.

events.label: Ahn typeface
events.note: The first widely used non-square, variable-width Hangul face, released as a computer font in 1991.

events.label: PostScript and the LaserWriter
events.note: Adobe's page-description language made outline type and pages device-independent, the base of desktop publishing.

events.label: Microsoft Windows 1.0
events.note: Started the path by which the GUI reached most of the world's PCs.

events.label: Fontographer
events.note: The first commercial Bézier font editor for a personal computer; anyone could now publish a typeface.

events.label: QuarkXPress
events.note: The layout program that dominated professional publishing in the 1990s and made layered, free-form spreads routine.

events.label: HyperCard
events.note: Bill Atkinson's card-and-button authoring tool prefigured the web and no-code design tools.

events.label: Seoul Olympics and the horizontal Hankyoreh
events.note: Korea's 1964 moment in design, the same year a national daily launched in horizontal Hangul setting.

events.label: NeXT Computer
events.note: Jobs's workstation with Display PostScript and the Dock; its OS became the foundation of Mac OS X and iOS.

events.label: Communist rule ends in Poland and Czechoslovakia
events.note: The market economy removes the state commissioning system that sustained the Polish and Czech poster schools.

events.label: Adobe Photoshop 1.0
events.note: Layered raster compositing put photographic collage and texture on every designer's desk, the engine of grunge.

events.label: Vignelli calls Emigre 'garbage'
events.note: Massimo Vignelli's attack in Print made the legibility wars between modernists and the digital avant-garde public.

events.label: World Wide Web goes public
events.note: Tim Berners-Lee's hypertext system, built on a NeXT, made the link the basic unit of screen design.

events.label: Ray Gun launched
events.note: David Carson's art direction took grunge typography from niche to newsstand.

events.label: NCSA Mosaic
events.note: The first popular browser to show images inline with text, turning web pages into graphic layouts.

events.label: Information Landscapes at TED5
events.note: Muriel Cooper's last demo showed typography moving in 3D space, a lost path for interface design.

events.label: Windows 95
events.note: The Start menu and taskbar fixed the desktop paradigm for a mass audience.

events.label: CSS Level 1
events.note: The W3C's 17 December recommendation separated presentation from structure, making web typography and layout designable.

events.label: Macromedia Flash 1.0
events.note: A vector animation plug-in that let designers make the web move for a decade.

events.label: Hong Kong handover
events.note: Colonial identities were renamed and redrawn, and cross-cultural design became Hong Kong's explicit subject.

events.label: Iranian Graphic Designers Society founded
events.note: Momayez's professional society rebuilds Iranian design's institutions after the revolution.

events.label: iMac G3
events.note: Translucent Bondi Blue plastic made consumer computing playful and set the Y2K look.

events.label: First Things First 2000 manifesto
events.note: Adbusters, Emigre, Eye and others reissued Garland's manifesto with 33 signatories, reopening the debate about design and consumerism.

events.label: Superflat exhibition, Parco Tokyo
events.note: Murakami's show and theory travelled to Los Angeles in 2001, reframing Japanese pop graphics as art.

events.label: Aqua unveiled
events.note: Apple's glossy, translucent Mac OS X interface opened a decade of rich, rendered UI.

events.label: AbiFarès publishes Arabic Typography
events.note: The first comprehensive modern sourcebook on Arabic type, written because none existed to teach from.

events.label: Processing
events.note: Reas and Fry's sketchbook language made code an everyday material for designers and artists.

events.label: CSS Zen Garden
events.note: One HTML file restyled by many designers proved CSS could carry real visual design.

events.label: Khatt Foundation founded
events.note: An Amsterdam foundation that became the hub for bilingual Arabic–Latin type design and research.

events.label: First Bienal Tipos Latinos
events.note: A travelling Latin American type biennial gives the region's type designers a shared stage.

events.label: Helvetica documentary
events.note: Gary Hustwit's film, featuring Experimental Jetset and Norm, marked neo-modernism's arrival as a public taste.

events.label: iPhone
events.note: Announced 9 January: multi-touch glass replaced keys, and skeuomorphic rendering stood in for touch.

events.label: App Store
events.note: Third-party apps turned interface design into a mass profession and a visual arms race.

events.label: iPad
events.note: Announced 27 January; its bookshelf and leather apps marked skeuomorphism's high-water mark.

events.label: Windows Phone 7 and Metro
events.note: Microsoft's typographic, flat phone interface brought Swiss principles to mobile.

events.label: Responsive Web Design
events.note: Ethan Marcotte's A List Apart article named fluid, device-agnostic layout.

events.label: Thoughts on Flash
events.note: Jobs's open letter explained why iOS would not run Flash, ending the Flash era's momentum.

events.label: V&A: Postmodernism, Style and Subversion 1970-1990
events.note: The V&A exhibition historicised postmodern design, from Memphis to Emigre, as a closed period.

events.label: Bootstrap
events.note: Twitter's open-source UI kit made a shared component system the default starting point of the web.

events.label: Forstall leaves Apple
events.note: His October departure put Jony Ive in charge of software design and ended Apple's skeuomorphic era.

events.label: Unified Arabic revived digitally
events.note: The 29LT foundry turns Khattar's 1947 reform into working digital fonts.

events.label: iOS 7
events.note: Announced 10 June, Apple's flat redesign made Swiss-derived minimalism the industry default.

events.label: Atomic Design
events.note: Brad Frost's post gave design systems a shared vocabulary of components.

events.label: Material Design
events.note: Announced 25 June at Google I/O, the first publicly documented, cross-platform design language at Google's scale.

events.label: Figma public release
events.note: A multiplayer, browser-based design tool made shared component libraries the working medium.

events.label: Fluent Design System
events.note: Microsoft added light, depth and translucent Acrylic to Metro's flatness.

events.label: Tokyo 2020 pictograms released
events.note: Masaaki Hiromura's team updated the 1964 pictogram heritage, later animated in the 2021 opening ceremony.

events.label: Flash end of life
events.note: Adobe ended Flash Player support on 31 December, closing the era formally.

events.label: Glassmorphism and macOS Big Sur
events.note: Michal Malewicz named the frosted-glass trend as Big Sur shipped translucent, depth-rich UI.

events.label: M+ opens in Hong Kong
events.note: Asia's first global museum of visual culture to collect graphic design from across East Asia.

events.label: Material You
events.note: Google's dynamic colour derived from the user's wallpaper made personalisation a system property.

events.label: Midjourney open beta
events.note: Opened 12 July via Discord, putting text-to-image generation in designers' hands.

events.label: ChatGPT
events.note: Released 30 November, it made conversation a mainstream interface and triggered the AI design era.

events.label: Apple Vision Pro
events.note: Released 2 February; visionOS's glass windows were the direct ancestor of Liquid Glass.

events.label: Vibe coding
events.note: Andrej Karpathy's February coinage named prompt-driven software making; Collins Word of the Year 2025.

events.label: Material 3 Expressive
events.note: Google's most researched update reintroduced emotion, shape and springy motion to Material.

events.label: Liquid Glass
events.note: Announced 9 June at WWDC, Apple's first cross-platform redesign since iOS 7, met with mixed-to-negative reviews.

events.label: Alan Dye leaves Apple for Meta
events.note: Apple's human-interface chief departed in December, months after shipping Liquid Glass.

events.label: Liquid Glass revised at WWDC 2026
events.note: Apple reduced default transparency and added a clear-to-tinted slider, a rare public course correction.
